epub_9.title: Kacey Musgraves, Crossover Queen
epub_9.text:
Kacey Musgraves, Crossover Queen
Goings On
Kacey Musgraves, Crossover Queen
Also: John David Washington plays a tech bro in “Disruption,” Samara Joy and Christian McBride perform at Central Park, Jacob Elordi’s stars in Ridley Scott’s latest movie, and more.
By Sheldon Pearce,Brian Seibert,Jane Bua,Rhoda Feng,Richard Brody
August 28, 2026
In the past few years,
country music has reëxerted its sway on the pop-music charts and the broader Zeitgeist they reflect, but the genre’s greatest crossover success story remains the Texas singer-songwriter
Kacey Musgraves
. Since her 2013 major-label début, “Same Trailer Different Park,” she has been a shaping voice of modern Americana, not just in the way her music marries rustic and cosmopolitan sensibilities but in its underlying progressive ideal. Clever, observant, and funny as hell, she is one of music’s sharpest lyricists, and a breakthrough in 2018, the kaleidoscopic disco-country masterpiece “Golden Hour,” expanded her creative world view, scaling up from small-town concerns to something more universal, winning Album of the Year at the Grammys in the process.
Musgraves’s subsequent albums have been sprawling in their search for meaning, and even more adventurous in the sonic pathways travelled to get there. “Star-Crossed,” from 2021, was a psychedelic divorce record that incorporated soft rock and dance music, while “Deeper Well,” from 2024, goes even more soft-spun for the songs of her Saturn return and its reassessed priorities, which included seeing the big picture. Her most recent album, “Middle of Nowhere,” is a homecoming, if not a full reset. Not only does its music scale back to the sounds of the country canon—bluegrass and Western swing, regional Mexican music such as norteño, and the Creole blues of zydeco, with plenty of acoustic guitar and pedal steel—it does so for meditations on how she defines herself as a woman and as an artist. Musgraves brings those conversations with her to the stage at
Madison Square Garden
, on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, as she continues her journey of self-discovery.—
Sheldon Pearce
About Town
Dance
In 2001, the
Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Company
prepared a work that was scheduled to première, on a stage between the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, on Sept. 12. The début did not happen, but, twenty-five years later, the company performs a new piece that reflects on that moment and all that has happened since. “Curriculum IV: Spin and Spin! Turn! Turn! Turn!,” the final offering of this year’s
River to River Festival
, features a live score by Samora Pinderhughes sourced from Nina Simone’s rendition of “Turn! Turn! Turn! (To Everything There Is a Season).” The free performances at Wagner Park also nod to the outdoor theatre’s presiding spirit, the Statue of Liberty.—
Brian Seibert (Robert F. Wagner, Jr., Park; Sept. 10, 12-13.)
Classical
This has been a big summer for moviegoing—“The Odyssey,” “Minions 3,” “Jackass 5,” “Scary Movie 6”—and the
Met Opera
wants in on the action. It’s reigniting its
annual
HD Festival
, screening live recordings of recent operas. Did you miss the Met’s début of Gabriela Lena Frank’s “El Último Sueño de Frida y Diego”? They’ve got you. What about “I Puritani,” the first new production of Bellini’s bel-canto masterwork that the Met has put on in almost fifty years? Breathe easy. Have you always been afraid to sneak to the rest room during Wagner’s nearly five-hour “Tristan und Isolde”? No sweat: the festival splits it up into two movies, a day apart. You’ll just have to wait twenty-four more hours for that chord to resolve.
—Jane Bua (Josie Robertson Plaza; Sept. 2-7.)
Off Broadway
The idea that “behind every great fortune is a great crime” gets a twist in Andrew Stein’s topical new artificial-unintelligence play,
“
Disruption
,”
in which a great fortune is about to be made through a series of moral crimes. Nick (John David Washington), a silky-smooth tech entrepreneur, invites three friends and their wives to invest in a new algorithm he’s developed, pitched as “Waze . . . but for your life.” Yet the unwitting guinea pigs are eerily reminiscent of what Daisy Hildyard calls “second bodies,” rather than ensouled beings. Their quiddities remain hazily drawn, snapping into focus only when required by Stein’s overdetermined plot; the rhizomatic spread of numbers across the stage floor—Zoë Hurwitz designed the set—reinforces that uncanny cybernetic quality.—
Rhoda Feng (Pershing Square Signature Center; through Oct. 4.)
Jazz
As the
City Parks Foundation’s SummerStage
winds to a close, the concert series saves some of its best for last, pairing the singer
Samara Joy
with the bassist and bandleader
Christian McBride
to celebrate the seventieth anniversary of the historic jazz label Verve Records. A Bronx native and six-time Grammy winner, Joy is among the most expressive jazz performers working, her satiny and sumptuous voice deployed sparingly. McBride, a fixture of the scene since the early nineties, has collaborated with artists across the spectrum, including Joy, on his most recent album, “Without Further Ado, Vol 1.” They are joined by a group of other musicians, led by Mei Semones, in honoring “Getz/Gilberto,” the classic 1964 album by João Gilberto and Stan Getz.—
Sheldon Pearce (Rumsey Playfield in Central Park; Sept. 2.)
Movies
Exquisite style and confrontational substance fuse to startling effect in Rafael Manuel’s teeming début feature,
“Filipiñana,”
which is set at a golf resort near Manila that’s a microcosm of modern political dysfunction. The story, which is told in comedically choreographed visual anecdotes, is centered on women who work there—caddies and so-called tee girls, whose underpaid labor puts them in close contact with wealthy, arrogant, and predatory men. The main drama involves a rural teen-age tee girl who recognizes the resort’s president as the potentate who evicted her family from their land. Rage stays wryly below the surface; Manuel sardonically delights in musical spectacles staged for guests, and the synchronized swinging of clubs at a driving range evokes the superficial charm of robotic lives.—
Richard Brody (Opening Aug. 28 at
Film Forum
, nationally Sept. 4.)
Movies
Ridley Scott brings admirable restraint to
“The Dog Stars,”
a post-apocalyptic drama set in Colorado in the near future, after a strain of influenza has killed most people. A mechanic named Hig (Jacob Elordi), who lives at an abandoned airstrip with a fierce military veteran (Josh Brolin), pilots a small plane to the ghost town of Denver, where he fetches supplies and visits the house he’d shared with his late wife. In his travels, he encounters a father-and-daughter pair of ranchers (Guy Pearce and Margaret Qualley) and tries to make contact with other survivors. The heart of the film—despite gory confrontations with feral marauders—is the rebuilding of trust, the overcoming of grief, and the importance of vaccines; the science-fiction premise morphs sweetly into sentimental melodrama.—
R.B. (In wide release.)
P.S. Good stuff on the internet:
Take a walk on the moon
It’s as good as everyone says
The 2026
Dogue
winner is peak cute

epub_10.title: A Tasting Menu That Uses Every Last Scrap
epub_10.text:
A Tasting Menu That Uses Every Last Scrap
The Food Scene
A Tasting Menu That Uses Every Last Scrap
At Cynthia, an emphasis on low-waste cooking yields a menu of thrilling abundance.
By Helen Rosner
August 16, 2026
At first, the most intriguing thing about Cynthia was that it made you work for it. Another upscale West Village restaurant in an ever-deepening sea of upscale West Village restaurants, Cynthia stood out by eschewing online reservation platforms in favor of old-fashioned e-mail. Send a note, wait for a reply, hope. I found this both intriguing and intimidating: the possibility of human rejection was far more daunting than a search result reading “No tables available for your selected date.” Fortunately for the anxious among us, and less fortunately for those still loyal to the dying rituals of interpersonal correspondence, Cynthia has recently moved to online reservations. A concession to scale? A move to boost business? Either way, the path to booking a table is easier now, and—considering how overtly excellent I found Cynthia to be—that’s entirely a good thing.
The restaurant, which opened in May, is a co-production between the restaurateur Claire DuBois and the chef Sherry Cardoso. Cardoso has a blue-chip pedigree (
Per Se
,
Brooklyn Fare
) but is best known, in the public imagination, for her star turn on the most recent season of “Top Chef,” in which she made it to the final three before losing, in a real nail-biter of a season finale. Cynthia is named for DuBois’s aunt, Cynthia Peck, the matriarch of the late Southern California stalwart Angelo’s and Vinci’s Ristorante, a red-sauce joint that she and her husband operated for decades. Unlike that spot, which was enormous and famed for a degree of raucousness, Cynthia is a tasting-menu restaurant, refined and notably tiny. You’ll likely brush elbows with your neighbors, and you’ll absolutely be able to eavesdrop on their conversation, though you might find yourself just too busy paying attention to the food, which is punchy, witty, and utterly thrilling.
The meal is listed as six courses (seven, if you spring for a Wagyu supplement, eighty dollars for two), but what you’re served is actually closer to a dozen, because several courses feature suites of dishes, built around shared ingredients and interconnecting elements. A corn course, for example, has three parts: first, a quenelle of corn ice cream, soft and summer-bright, set over ribbons of marinated summer squash, confettied with fluffy shaved foie gras and bits of nori. Next, kernels of corn stud a beurre blanc draped over faceted hunks of summer squash with sweetly charred edges. Last, and almost dessert-like, is an intensely concentrated corn posset, dense and rich as cream cheese, under a cloud of sheep’s-milk-cheese foam and a dark dusting of the corn’s burnt husk. The dish is finished with a blob of caviar—the good stuff, platinum osetra. For once, in this caviar-obsessed town, a dish that justifies the use of roe by properly framing its delicate salinity.
Each of those corn preparations was entirely successful on its own; each could have served as a full course, a started-and-finished thought. I felt the same way about the lobster, which came in two parts: hunks of firm tail meat were served in a Thai-inflected red curry, intensely herbaceous and rich with coconut milk, and scattered with fresh-shaved black truffle; the more tender meat of the claw and knuckle was presented in a “taco,” with a tortilla made of pressed plantain, one of the menu’s many nods to Cardoso’s Brazilian upbringing. In the finale of “Top Chef,” one of Cardoso’s mentors warned her away from presenting multi-dish courses, lest one dish overshadow another. The only time this happened at Cynthia, though, was in the supplementary course of A5 Wagyu, a three-parter, in which a brisket-filled dumpling and a B.L.T.-inspired roulade of thinly sliced tongue both felt like drab afterthoughts compared to the main event: glimmering slices of rib eye, impossibly well marbled, served with creamy dollops of eggplant purée. Maybe the abundance just works better in a restaurant than it does at a judges’ table; there is an animalistic delight in being on the receiving end of so much thoughtful variety, even if, by the end of the proceedings, you may be approaching an Adephagian degree of stuffed.
Helen, Help Me!
E-mail your questions
about dining, eating, and anything food-related, and Helen may respond in a future newsletter.
Cardoso’s approach also lends itself quite elegantly to another element of Cynthia’s culinary philosophy, an emphasis on low-waste cooking. Some ingredient scraps and stems are ferried off to the bar, where they infuse liquors or ferment into
tepache
. Others are stewed with aromatics and oil to make a riotous take on XO sauce, funky and inky and complex, which gilds the hunks of squash under their corny beurre blanc. Bits of pickled veg and infused butters come with the bread course, and the Parker House-like bread itself is multicolored thanks to leftover bits of beet and ramp and carrot. Even the seeds strained out of lemon juice are pressed into service in a marmalade that’s given to diners as a little take-home treat. This is sustainability theatre, a convoluted puzzle of ingredient inputs and outputs that is entirely unsustainable as a way to actually live—unless you have a kitchen staff and a room of paying customers. Still, it’s awfully entertaining to see all the clever ways Cynthia pulls it off.
As at many tasting-menu restaurants, you’ll receive your menu only at the end of your meal. To begin, instead, each diner is presented with a card printed with something between a manifesto and a poem: “There is no summer quite like a New York summer,” it begins, and continues with a litany of the attributes of eggplant, tomato, watermelon, et al. Honestly, it’s fiddle-faddle, self-serious and not nearly poetic enough; a meal that’s this well executed doesn’t need all that throat-clearing. In recent weeks, the restaurant has added an à-la-carte menu—it’s available only at the bar, which takes up a third of the petite room. I won’t argue the wisdom of that as a financial choice—can any restaurant survive these days if it doesn’t offer a burger?—but it does risk dampening Cynthia’s special, strange, sui-generis specificity. At the close of dinner, after all of those double and triple dishes, dessert arrives in the singular, and I don’t need a poem to convey the beauty of its simplicity: a swirling scoop of watermelon sorbet served on top of coconut foam and crowned with cubes of cantaloupe and honeydew. I can see it, and taste it, right there on the plate. ♦

epub_11.title: Three Books That Will Transport You
epub_11.text:
Three Books That Will Transport You
What We’re Reading
Three Books That Will Transport You
By Katy Waldman
August 19, 2026
I’m going through a phase lately
where almost everything reminds me of “
Adam’s Curse
,” by William Butler Yeats. The poem is about how our most worthwhile pursuits—things like art, love, and beauty—often seem to demand a measure of toil. Or, as a woman in the poem wistfully puts it, how “we must labour to be beautiful.” The speaker reflects that “I strove / To love you in the old high way of love.” He sounds tired from the effort.
Then I read my colleague
Hanif Abdurraqib’s gorgeous essay
about our collective longing for inconvenience, in which he discusses a friend who “wants to fall in love
the old-fashioned way
,” meaning without using a dating app. I thought immediately, “The curse!” Abdurraqib’s point, though, appears to be that the curse might be a blessing in disguise, or at least that our attempts to outrun the curse might be more cursed than the curse itself. (Yeats, proto-friction-maxxer that he seems to be, might agree: the poem ends on the image of a “hollow moon,” an emblem of empty, unsatisfying escapism if there ever was one.)
So when I was asked, by this newsletter’s editor, to recommend some “transporting” summer reads, I wanted, in the spirit of the curse, to highlight a few books whose transports can’t be separated from their “inconvenient” qualities: unconventionality, abstruseness, even unresolved emotional pain. I hope you love them in the old high way of love.
“
Orbital
,” by Samantha Harvey
Harvey’s novel centers on a group of six astronauts living in an international space station, hundreds of miles above Earth. No crisis hits, aliens don’t attack, the fuel supply is fine. Rather than a conventional setup-climax-dénouement plot, we get eerily domestic moments aboard the shuttle, affecting scraps of the characters’ memories, some of the most dazzling descriptions of light I’ve ever read—imagine Dante’s “Paradiso” with a secular overlay, as if space were simultaneously the seventh heaven and Earth’s untended back yard—and a sense of being out of history and time (“the whipcrack of morning arrives every ninety minutes,” Harvey writes). The novel—an astonishing work of humanism sheathed in an escapist premise—should be required reading for every faux-utopian tech stooge who wants to loot the planet so their A.I. systems can displace and replace people. (Not that I’m mad about it!)
“
The Sense of an Ending
,” by Frank Kermode
My editor recommended this book to me after I pitched her a somewhat convoluted essay idea. She thought Kermode’s formal analysis of delay and catharsis in classic literary texts might be useful. Not only was it
highly
useful (I abandoned the essay idea), it was thrilling, dense, complex, absorbing—and a real struggle to get through. I had to sit for a long time with individual sentences, in part because they demanded to be reality-tested against my own perceptions and in part because that’s what it took for me to understand them. Such deep concentration caused me to lose track of my surroundings—a true escape.
“
A Truce That Is Not Peace
,” by Miriam Toews
This book’s “inciting incident” is that, in order to participate in a conference, Toews has to answer the question “Why do you write?” Her mind returns to two formative events: the deaths, by suicide, of her father and sister, both of whom walked in front of trains. The experience of losing these family members, Toews shows, organizes her art, the way she is always hoping somehow, through language, to resurrect her loved ones, even as she insists she can’t. She expresses a preference for silence over false speech—a scorn for easy fictions is something she shared with her father and sister—but not over true speech, or true writing. Does this memoir, about some of the worst things that can happen to a person, offer escape? Sure—of the kind more commonly known as art.
Our editors and critics choose the most captivating, notable, brilliant, surprising, absorbing, weird, thought-provoking, and talked-about books.
