Still, this fact is easily set aside when so many forces play on a parent’s fears. Ultra-processed foods make up more than half of our daily calorie intake. Microplastics are in our water and in our bodies, and the consequences are unclear. Rates of autism are rising to previously unseen levels, owing largely to better detection and new diagnostic criteria, but the numbers are still disconcerting. Autoimmune conditions are becoming more prevalent, and we don’t fully understand why. Pharmaceutical companies are driven by a desire for profits, not just the well-being of our children. Medical care is prohibitively expensive. Expert guidance is constantly changing: the theory that
covid
originated from a lab leak is disinformation, then suddenly it becomes the official stance of Joe Biden’s F.B.I. and his Department of Energy. Tylenol is safe for pregnant mothers, then Trump says that it’s not. It can be hard to know whom to trust.
MAHA
promises answers. In the world of “crunchy” (alternative, natural) parenting—as opposed to “silky” (conventional, medicinal) or “scrunchy” (a hybrid)—there is a holistic remedy for almost any ailment. There is also genuine community and care and, tucked inside of that, a heady feeling of ascension: the knowledge that you have set yourself apart from a consumerist, toxic mainstream—or, as a group of social scientists studying vaccine hesitancy in Australia termed it, the Unhealthy Other. A mother in Virginia named Lindsay Logan told me that, when she was eight months pregnant, she attended a private screening, arranged by a mom friend, of “Vaxxed II: The People’s Truth,” a movie produced by Kennedy. The theatre was cool and dark. Surrounded by like-minded mothers, watching footage of crying babies, she felt overcome by a certainty that, having chosen not to vaccinate, she was living the right way. “You’re, like, ‘I’m so glad I’ve been enlightened,’ ” she told me. “I wasn’t one of the sheep.”
“Know better, do better” is a popular
MAHA
mantra, another way of saying D.Y.O.R., or “do your own research.” This means turning to the internet to learn about red dyes, additives, food as medicine, essential oils, and when to apply a garlic poultice to the bottom of your feet. It also means knowing how to read vaccine inserts, the technical fine print on vaccine packaging. On parenting forums, mothers remind one another that no one cares about your child more than you do. On Facebook, discussion groups foster the feeling of a countercultural underground. Pages are shut down for promoting misinformation, then reappear under new names. Conversation takes place under the veil of coded language: vaccines are referred to as “vak seens” or, more commonly, with a cupcake emoji.
The descent into a full-blown
MAHA
life style can be swift. Heather Lindstrom-Hamilton, a mother in Thousand Oaks, a wealthy city outside Los Angeles, was thirty-nine when her husband received a cancer diagnosis. He died six months later, and Lindstrom-Hamilton was suddenly a widow caring for four children. Looking for answers about her husband’s death, she was “low-hanging fruit for the anti-vax world,” she told me. She came to believe that toxins had caused his cancer. She changed her diet and began telling her kids, “We don’t eat cancer, and we don’t drink cancer.”
Soon, she fell in with a group of anti-vax moms. She recalled once driving to Ojai to pay a doctor around two thousand dollars for vaccine-exemption cards for two of her kids. She gave herself coffee enemas and took her children to a holistic chiropractor, who told her that, if their bodies were in alignment, they wouldn’t be as vulnerable to illness. Chiropractors have asserted themselves as a
MAHA
-safe alternative to modern medicine. Lindstrom-Hamilton pointed me to the website of a prominent “pediatric and prenatal” chiropractor named Stanton Hom. He publicly calls himself “Dr Stanton Hom,” even though he is not a medical doctor. (Hom did not respond to requests for comment.) On his website, new patients are directed to a video of Hom introducing himself by saying, “So let’s be honest: if you’re here, something fully isn’t right.”
Lindstrom-Hamilton left the anti-vax movement during the pandemic. Her moment of revelation came while tuning in to the live stream of a pastor she watched every night, Rob McCoy (the former pastor of Charlie Kirk), as he interviewed a plastic surgeon about
covid
. “I had this cognitive dissonance of, like, ‘Wait a minute, we’re in a pandemic, and I’m listening to a guy that does boob jobs?’ ” she told me. She began what she now calls “my unlearning phase.” Years later, she still has a house full of expensive supplements that she no longer uses. When I asked her what she used to consume, she sent me a list of forty-three products and protocols. “It was exhausting,” Lindstrom-Hamilton said.
It does not take long to notice that much of
MAHA
is trying to sell you something. A formerly vaccine-hesitant mother named Brandie Hadfield, who lives in Toronto, told me that her pursuit of natural parenting involved spending about a decade of her life in a multilevel-marketing company called Juice Plus+, which sells capsules that it claims offer antioxidants from powdered fruits and vegetables. (Joe Schwarcz, a chemistry professor at McGill University, reviewed a study on Juice Plus+ and found that two of its capsules have the antioxidant power of only “about two to three bites of an apple.” A Juice Plus+ spokesperson said that the company’s products provide “added nutrition” but “aren’t meant to replace fruits and vegetables.”)
MAHA
encourages a certain entrepreneurial hustle. Heather Simpson, another mom who left the anti-vax movement, showed me a crew-neck sweatshirt that she had designed to sell to her followers, printed with key terms in millennial fonts: “
elderberry syrup
,” “
colloidal silver
.” The life style is up for sale on a grand scale, too. There are “agrihoods,” where families can live in healthful community with one another, including one in Georgia called Serenbe. Its founder recently claimed that none of the two hundred and forty children growing up in the community suffer from asthma, thanks to an emphasis on chemical-free living.
Lindstrom-Hamilton observed that the commodification of
MAHA
often involves rich women—in “perfect white farmhouses, with their perfectly dressed children in beige clothes”—selling their way of life to non-rich women online. After following one popular influencer on Instagram, I received an automated D.M.: “Hey friend 🫶 So glad you are here.” She had an arsenal of coupon codes to help me make a “clean swap” to a nontoxic household. While browsing, I could also watch a nine-minute video of her home birth.
This year, a D.C.-based nonprofit embarked on a study to understand what, exactly,
MAHA
has become. Among its findings was the fact that phrases like “the research shows” or “follow the science,” when deployed to combat
MAHA
talking points, are instead perceived as versions of “you think I’m stupid.” During a briefing about their study, the researchers charted the typical path of a “worried mom” who goes online looking for answers. “The more beliefs she begins to adopt, the more the liberal community moves away/scorns her, the further she gets pulled down the pipeline,” the researchers explained. They called this phenomenon the “radicalization funnel.”
Michael and Leah met on the internet. He was living in northern Virginia and played bass in an eighties-metal cover band called Bad Habit. She lived in Texas and followed the band on MySpace. She sent him a friend request on Facebook, and he messaged her and told her that she was beautiful. In 2012, around the time that he turned twenty-one, he flew to Texas to meet her. He gave her a T-shirt that said “
Someone in Virginia Loves Me
” and, eventually, a one-way plane ticket to join him on the East Coast. As a couple, they looked like they’d arrived from another decade. Michael wore bell-bottoms, and his hair was long and curly, like Leah’s. He remembered thinking,
How often do you find people who are into old-school rock and roll
? They listened to the same records and went to shows together. “It was real simple, but that’s what we did,” Michael said. “It felt like love.” As far as he knew, Leah wasn’t particularly interested in health or wellness. But, from the start of their relationship, she was clear that the thing she wanted most in life was to become a mother.
Michael was not so sure about becoming a father. When he was born, he was given the name Gerald Lester Horrocks III, in honor of his father and his father’s father. But both men had problems with alcohol. His dad, who worked in construction, “drank heavy—real, real heavy,” Michael said. He decided that he wasn’t going to be the same way. After high school, he wrote a list of names next to a picture of himself in a notebook. He liked the name Rick, but he didn’t think he looked like a Rick. The only name that seemed to fit was Michael. He tried it out for a year, shortened Lester to Lee, then legally became Michael Lee Horrocks. He took whatever “crappy jobs” he could find. He worked at a plastics factory, a book press, a Home Depot distribution center. “I didn’t have a lot going through my head back then,” he said. “It was more like ‘Where’s my next joint coming from? What’s the next record? Who are we jamming with?’ That was all I did. We’re talking about a person who thought he made it if he got his forklift license.”
Michael and Leah had an outdoor wedding in 2016, holding hands under an arbor draped in greenery. Leah was old-fashioned about most things in life, especially marriage and kids—her “dream and desire.” But she had begun to feel that facets of mainstream feminism were set up to mock that life style. Leah wanted to be a stay-at-home mother, and Michael was mostly supportive of the idea. “We had a ‘You name the babies, I name the dog’ kind of thing,” he said. Two years after they were married, Keith was born. Leah called him the “sunshine of my life.”
In our conversations, Leah spoke frequently about her “transformation, awakening, activation, whatever you wanna call it.” These shifts started during the pandemic, when she was pregnant with Donnie. Michael, who had been following the emergence of the virus in China through his favorite news source, a conservative aggregator called Citizen Free Press, thought that the pandemic “didn’t smell right” and that
covid
was “make-believe.” His work at gas stations continued during lockdowns, and he watched with bewilderment as people unquestioningly followed government mask mandates and as plastic barriers went up around the cash register where he bought cigarettes.
When the
covid
vaccine became available, he and Leah declined to get it. “Michael was the very first person in 2020 to have me questioning vaccines,” Leah told me. (Michael said that his concern was with the federal government pushing a relatively untested new vaccine, not with “the normal shit that we have all gotten for years.”) On Instagram, where Leah was a part of a “sixties-seventies hippie community,” some of the people on her feed were “screaming, ‘Wear your mask’ ”; others were saying, “Don’t vaccinate your kids.” Leah started to post about her vaccine hesitancy. The more she did, the more polarizing her account became, which hardened her skepticism. Online, she met a woman who said that her son had started seizing and vomiting because of a vaccine. The woman claimed that, afterward, a doctor had pulled her aside and warned her that vaccines weren’t as safe as they seemed. The story terrified Leah. When Donnie was born, she didn’t vaccinate him.
Then, in the spring of 2021, Leah’s elderly grandmother died. Before her death, she had received two doses of the
covid
vaccine. Leah blamed the vaccine for her death. “I know everyone dies eventually, but it didn’t have to be right now,” she wrote at the time. A few days later, she posted a picture mimicking pro-vaccine frames that people were adding to their Facebook profile pictures. Hers said “
PROUDLY UNVACCINATED
.” In the caption, she reintroduced herself to the world, as if reborn: “I’m Leah. I’m a mother. I used to follow blindly and trust in the system with out question.” She added, “Now I feel superhuman.”
She quickly gained a following of anti-vaxxers. On TikTok, she held up a sign that read “
My body, my choice
.” “I’m no longer your product,” she wrote. “I am aware and ready to fight.” She increasingly characterized her choice to be a stay-at-home mom as an act of defiance. Michael noticed that she began buying organic groceries and talking about the dangers that red dyes posed to their kids. “I’d get hollered at for giving them red lollipops,” he said. “Then, all of a sudden, groceries were twice as much, because we’re buying organic ketchup.” Soon, pregnant with Star, Leah introduced herself to her followers once again, this time wearing a “
DEFUND FAUCI
” T-shirt. “I’m Leah,” the post began. “Apparently now I am a ‘raging conspiracy theorist’ and an ‘anti vaxxer.’ ”
At the time, Michael and Leah were living in a tiny, unincorporated community in West Virginia called Yellow Spring, set in a system of river valleys and forested ridges. Star was born on the couch in the living room. By then, Michael was spending more time away from home, on his motorcycle. Leah was the parent who fed the children, changed their diapers, bathed them, and planned to homeschool them. Michael didn’t question these choices. It wasn’t until Donnie received a diagnosis of S.M.A., a few months after his second birthday, that Michael began to ask about the children’s medical care. Donnie had started receiving an injection of a medication called Spinraza every four months. Before Spinraza’s release, in 2016, S.M.A. was the leading genetic cause of infant mortality, and there was no approved treatment. The medicine was capable of stabilizing the disease—an actual miracle drug.
To be suddenly reliant on a medication “was very difficult, being somebody who is more natural-minded,” Leah said. She shared the news of the diagnosis with her followers: she remained a “ ‘crunchy’ mama,” she wrote, “but there is a time and place for modern medicine.” She still posted about raw milk, immune-boosting smoothies, and, as the 2024 election approached, R.F.K., Jr., and a coming “great awakening.” After Trump won, she defended those who had voted for him. She posted pictures of the sky, searching for chemtrails. “The rabbit holes run deep,” she wrote, “but once you know, you know and it all makes so. much. sense.”
In the spring of 2025, Michael noticed Leah using a messaging app that he didn’t recognize. She seemed increasingly preoccupied with her phone, sometimes tucking it away when he approached. He thought that she was cheating on him. “I would have preferred that, honestly,” he said. “It would have been so much easier to explain.”
Late one night, he took Leah’s phone to the garage behind the house and opened it. For months, he learned, she had been using WhatsApp to correspond not with a lover but with an unnamed woman who had been acting as some kind of spiritual adviser and healer. He thumbed through the messages, taking screenshots as he went.
The healer warned of “evil activities going on in the world” and offered various cleansings on Leah’s behalf. She volunteered a “protective juju” to intercept a “coming attack.” She promised to “wash the poison” from Leah’s body and talked of procuring fresh herbs with healing properties, along with a calabash for a “voodoo” to bury in the yard. Leah and the adviser called each other “sis” or “sister”; the adviser referred to Michael’s mother as a “witch.” Michael saw that the adviser had frequently asked for payments in bitcoin, ranging from fifteen to more than a hundred dollars, and that Leah, at the adviser’s request, had provided her financial-account information. In the messages, both parties referred to these payments as offerings. “It was instantly, like, ‘Whoa, what the fuck is going on?’ ” Michael said.
MAHA
has many side quests, and adherents sometimes fall into multilevel-marketing schemes, buy supplements promising miracle cures, or take advice from A.I.-generated doctors and healers. Some diversions are more unorthodox. The world of spellwork scams has been documented at length on Reddit, where users report paying anonymous healers for palm readings and magical cleansings. On Etsy, self-described psychics and witches peddle spells promising success, luck, money, revenge, weight loss, and more specific outcomes such as “make him cry and beg for you” and “punish everyone who wronged you.” Leah told me that she had met her “spiritual guide” on social media. The money, she said, was never much, and anything she spent was for her children’s benefit. “I was trying to protect my kids,” she said.
To Michael, it looked like an “obvious scam.” In one exchange, Leah appeared to request help with something irritating Donnie’s skin:
Healer
: Donnie is healing now
Leah
: Okay I’m worried because he’s still really itchy and Michael is getting concerned and telling me to take him to be seen.
In another, she seemed to be making a payment on Donnie’s behalf:
Leah
: Offering for Donnie 🙏
Healer
: Offering received with thanks 🙏 I thought I said 20
Leah
: You said yesterday whatever I could. I sent $15 but there’s fees for purchasing Bitcoin . . . I will be sending you more soon sister 🙏
Healer
: What time tomorrow.
Michael was furious, most of all about the money. They were already facing foreclosure on their house. “My biggest enemy is right here in my back yard,” he said. That same night, another crisis was unfolding. Keith had traces of blood in his urine. Michael told me that, early the next morning, he tried to sneak Keith out of the house for a doctor’s appointment. But Leah caught them in the driveway, getting into a car with Michael’s mother, who cursed at Leah. In response, Leah called her a witch.
By then, the couple’s relationship was effectively over. That afternoon, Michael filed for an emergency protective order, claiming that Leah had struck him in the face during an argument. Later, according to court documents, Leah alleged that Michael had once “grabbed her by the neck and left a bruise on her hip.” She told me that she also considered the relationship to be emotionally abusive, which Michael denies. (A report by a lawyer appointed to represent the children noted that there were no allegations of violence against the kids and that Child Protective Services had concluded that they were safe with both parents.) Regardless, for a period of sixteen days, Michael was given temporary custody. Leah was devastated. The separation was traumatic for her and, she feared, for the children. She told me that they had never spent a night apart from her before. Star, then two years old, was still nursing.
Divorce proceedings began, and, not long after, Michael started dating Brianna, whom he met through the Kneepatch page. She had her own spiritual interests and offered online tarot readings and consultations for energy awakenings and for “twin flame” connections—a type of “profound spiritual bond” between two people who share a “soul energy,” as her website says. Dating Bri, Michael said, was like having “a personal psychologist.” She helped him define his style as “free-range parenting,” as opposed to “helicopter parenting.”
Michael believed that the judge in his divorce case, who’d once worked as a registered nurse, would side with him. (Early on, she ordered that “neither party shall discuss witchcraft with the children.”) But the result was mixed. The judge ruled that Michael and Leah would share custody of the children. Michael would take the kids three weekends a month during the school year, plus various holidays and birthdays; they would spend the rest of the time with Leah. But, against Leah’s wishes, the judge ordered that Keith attend public school instead of being homeschooled. That meant meeting school vaccination requirements. The laws in West Virginia were strict. Leah couldn’t get an exemption.
According to the custody agreement, Michael and Leah were supposed to make medical decisions together. If they couldn’t agree, they were to “follow the recommendations of the doctor.” But Michael and Leah couldn’t agree on what kind of doctor the kids should see, or when they should see one. Months later, when the red blotches appeared on Donnie’s face, Michael believed that this was exactly the kind of thing that he’d been fighting to prevent.
Nothing will test
MAHA
’s hold on so many Americans like the reëmergence of vaccine-preventable diseases. Last year, as measles cases increased, Lindsay Logan, the mom who attended the screening of “Vaxxed II,” became consumed with thoughts about her unvaccinated daughter being exposed to the virus. During family trips, while riding on public transportation or using a rest stop, she would think,
This is it
.
This is when we’re getting measles
. Earlier this year, she scheduled an appointment to get her daughter an M.M.R. shot. She kept it a secret from her
MAHA
mom friends, afraid of what they might think. As the date approached, she grew more and more fearful. The day before the visit, she took pictures and videos of her daughter—a record of her pre-vaccinated state—because, she said, “I was convinced that the next day, when she got the shot, I might not have the same child.”
Across the country, pediatricians have watched in horror as Kennedy’s H.H.S. has weakened the public’s faith in vaccination. He has released a new childhood vaccine schedule (which has since been blocked by a federal judge) that cut the number of recommended shots from seventeen to eleven. He has said that he personally ordered the C.D.C. to change its long-standing public guidance stating that vaccines do not cause autism. The agency’s website now says that this assertion is not “evidence-based,” because studies cannot definitively rule out the possibility that they do. Trump, meanwhile, has encouraged the vaccine debate. He recently signed an executive order calling for “maximal parental choice over vaccines.” At the signing, he spoke about vaccines in menacing terms, evoking images of “vats of vaccine” and “fluid”—“what seemingly looks like gallons”—being “pumped into your child’s body.” The combined three-in-one M.M.R. shot, he claimed, can be “quite lethal” and “explosive.”
This year, vaccination rates among kindergartners decreased across immunizations for measles, mumps, rubella, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis. New parents are also increasingly declining a Vitamin K injection for their infants. The shot has been standard for newborns since 1961. A so-called black-box warning associated with the shot mentions adverse reactions and has become a major topic among crunchy-parenting groups online. But the warning refers primarily to allergic reactions in adults; only one case of an allergic reaction has ever been recorded in a newborn. There is virtually no downside to the injection apart from the transient pain of the needle, and the upside is tremendous. Babies are born with low amounts of Vitamin K, which is required to form blood clots. Without the shot, an otherwise healthy newborn can bleed to death internally, usually in the brain.
This is what Stefani Leavitt, a Ph.D. student in Washington State, learned after giving birth to her second child. She had decided to deliver the baby at a birthing center, to avoid the temptation of an epidural. At one of her preparatory appointments, she was handed a form about Vitamin K, which she soon forgot about. “I am not someone who refuses vaccines,” Leavitt said. But she was overwhelmed caring for her first child, and never looked into it. When her second child, Olive, was born, no one mentioned the Vitamin K injection. Olive was about a month old when Leavitt noticed “little bruises” on her body and head. A few days later, she wouldn’t wake up from a nap. Leavitt rushed her to the hospital, where doctors found that her skull was filling with blood. She nearly died. Today, Olive has autism and epilepsy, and experiences several seizures a week. Leavitt told me that she has empathy for mothers who are overloaded with medical choices. “I understand why it’s happening,” she said. “But I just want to be, like, ‘Your child could die.’ ”
Some vaccine-preventable diseases are illnesses that today’s doctors have never treated firsthand. Deborah Greenhouse, a pediatrician in South Carolina, saw several babies with fatal cases of whooping cough when she was a resident. One coughed and gagged until it turned blue. “You don’t forget that,” she said. Alexandra Cvijanovich, a pediatrician in New Mexico, once assisted with a case of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis—a rare, deadly form of brain inflammation that typically develops seven to ten years after a case of measles. The patient had caught measles as a baby, when he was too young to be vaccinated. Then, when he was twelve, his brain suddenly began to shut down. It was “the worst death I’ve dealt with in my career,” Cvijanovich said.
Measles is one of the world’s most contagious diseases. Infected people typically recover within about two weeks. The danger lies in how quickly it can turn. For every thousand children infected, between one and three die from respiratory and neurological complications. In most states, measles-vaccination rates have fallen below the level required for herd immunity. Last year, an outbreak in West Texas killed two children. Two more deaths, in Pennsylvania, were recorded late this August. Earlier this year, South Carolina became the site of the country’s largest outbreak since the virus was declared eliminated, in 2000. It took nearly seven months to contain. In the meantime, another outbreak was under way in Utah—including in a small city called Vernal. One day, when a high-school student there reported that she was feeling feverish, her mother, a stay-at-home mommy blogger named Tamsyn Spackman, knew immediately that it was measles.
On her blog, Spackman describes herself as “a bit of a maverick” and “Dr Mom.” She writes about practicing “natural parenting” with her eight children, who range in age from infancy to eighteen years old. Spackman was vaccinated, but none of her children were. Within weeks, seven of the kids were sick. Fever came, then Koplik’s spots, then the telltale rash. Spackman spent about a thousand dollars on herbs, tinctures, and oils. These included yarrow, feverfew, catnip, elderberry, burdock root, licorice root, valerian root, pleurisy root, redroot, and zinc.
The kids recovered, but Spackman herself soon got sick. She waited for the rash—“a sign that the body has won,” as she wrote on her blog—but it never arrived. Instead, she had a recurring fever for about four weeks. Spackman told me that measles itself wasn’t “that scary.” She believed that, with the right natural approach, the virus could pass through the body like a “cleanse.” But, after weeks of her managing the illness at home, Spackman’s husband finally asked whether she had any “emotions” that she needed to work through. She admitted that she was, in fact, afraid. “I talked about some of those things, and I cried a little bit,” she said. That night, she took a hot bath, administered an herbal enema, drank teas to help her sweat, wrapped herself in a cold, wet sheet, and then went to bed. The next day, she said that the “deep ache I’ve had in my bones” was gone. “I’m finally, finally on the mend.”
“If you or your child have measles, you can: Rest.” Michael came home from the urgent-care center with an informational packet that included this advice. It also advised drinking fluids, taking Tylenol, and staying in a cool, dimly lit room. But mostly, it seemed, he had to wait. The next day, he took Keith and Star to a pediatric urgent-care unit to be tested for measles. The medical staff told Michael that Star’s oxygen level was below ninety per cent—dangerously low. An ambulance was already on the way.
Star was placed on a tiny stretcher, with tubes hooked up to her wrist and nose. Doctors tended to her in face masks and isolation gowns. They told Michael that Star had pneumonia—a common measles complication—and RSV, another respiratory virus. Once she was evaluated, she was taken to a second hospital, in Leesburg, Virginia, where the doctors held her overnight. Michael was “stressed to the absolute max,” he said. That evening, he “slept like a cat at the foot of her little bed.”
The next day, Leah drove to the hospital to be with Star, while Michael returned home to take care of the boys. Keith had been improving, but Donnie started getting worse. He coughed small, weak coughs. It sounded like his lungs were full. One day, Michael said, Donnie woke up from a nap and was “burning hot.” Michael checked his temperature; the thermometer read a hundred and five. Then he checked his oxygen; the oximeter said eighty-one per cent. Michael grabbed him, rushed out of the house, and blew through several red lights on the way to the hospital. He left the truck running with the doors open in the parking lot. “I was panicked,” he told me. The doctors said that Donnie had pneumonia in one of his lungs. Because of his S.M.A., he didn’t have the muscle to cough out the mucus. Another ambulance arrived.
By then, the children’s illness had become the subject of a battle online. Leah’s mother had posted first. If Donnie had measles, she wrote, he got it “from the ‘vaccinated’ kids” who went to public school with Keith. “The doctors visits have been almost every week and yet they tell us vaccinated kids are healthier! Hum!” Michael responded in a lengthy post on the Kneepatch page, with screenshots of his text messages with Leah and a picture of Donnie staring at the ceiling, his arm folded on his tiny chest, his face covered in red spots: “Y’all send some prayers our way [for] Donnie today. He is currently being tested for measles. I have fought tooth and nail in court to get my children vaxxed especially Donnie.” He added, “I’m so upset it’s hard to get into words.” Comments accumulated, some torching Leah’s parenting. But, as the days went by, Michael didn’t post an update on the test results. “So . . . .,” one follower asked, “did they test positive for measles or not?”
What Michael didn’t say was that, sometime after Star’s hospital visit, the kids’ nose swabs had come back negative for measles. PCR tests for measles are considered generally reliable, though false negatives do happen. I asked several doctors to review an account of the children’s symptoms, along with a photo of Donnie’s rash. They told me that the professionals who had treated the kids as if they had measles had been right to do so. But it’s also possible that the kids had something else. Other illnesses can produce fever and rash: rubella, HHV-6, parvovirus, scarlet fever. Michael could have arranged for an antibody test, but he didn’t pursue it. Even after the test results came back, he and Brianna believed that the culprit was measles. “There were 8+ doctors over the course of this situation, in VERY different hospitals, that ALL diagnosed them with Measles,” Brianna eventually wrote to Michael’s followers. “It would be VERY weird for it to be anything else.” Her own three children—all vaccinated—had shared a house with Michael’s for a few days at the beginning of spring break, and they never caught so much as a sniffle. Keith, who was vaccinated, had a milder case. What else, they reasoned, could explain this?
Leah was not moved by these arguments. She believed that Michael had seized on whatever explanation would benefit his custody appeal in court. “This came out of nowhere and you think this is a coincidence due to ME not vaccinating our kids?” she texted him. “No dude. Absolutely not.” At the start of the ordeal, she had accused Michael of spiritual manipulation. “Sounds like your witches have been at work,” she texted him. But she had also asked reasonable questions about how this could have happened when there were no confirmed cases of the illness in West Virginia at the time. “Logically speaking, I wouldn’t think it’s the measles if no one else has it, but who knows?” she wrote. When the tests came back negative, she felt vindicated. Now who didn’t trust the science?
They had the test results, but little had changed. They were still living in two different realities, unable to agree on the truth. Donnie spent a night in the hospital, then was released. A couple of days later, the boys finally returned to their mom’s house. Spring break was over.
What should be done when parents differ on whether to vaccinate a child? I spoke to several mothers who said that the more they committed to a
MAHA
life style, the more it strained their relationship. Lindsey Fergins, a forty-two-year-old mom in Ohio, told me that she almost lost her marriage as a result. “It caused a huge rift between myself and my husband,” Fergins said. Around 2019, it became the focus of their couples counselling. “It got to the point where, if I had found out that he went to take our daughter to get a vaccine against my will, I would have divorced him,” she said. During the pandemic, though, Fergins found that she was more scared of the virus than of the vaccine. She discovered a Facebook group for women who’d left the anti-vax movement. She sat her husband down, apologized, and told him that they needed to get their kids caught up on their vaccines. “He was just speechless,” Fergins said. “It was a turning point in our marriage.”
Other times, disagreements end in legal action. One such case, in 2017, centered on a mother in Michigan named Rebecca Bredow, who did not want to vaccinate her son. Her ex-husband, James Horne, did. Bredow’s lawyer signed a consent order on her behalf agreeing to vaccinate the child, but Bredow ignored it. Bredow was held in contempt and handcuffed, and spent five days in jail. She later claimed that Horne never cared about vaccines at all—he had just used the issue to secure a better custody deal. The case made Horne a target of the anti-vax community. Del Bigtree, an activist close to R.F.K., Jr., once followed Horne through an airport, filming as he asked questions like “Is your son’s health really what matters to you?”
The central legal inquiry of any custody dispute involves determining what’s in the “best interest of the child.” This is a broad, flexible standard—and it’s up to a judge to decide. Dorit Reiss, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies cases involving vaccine disputes, told me that judges sometimes favor the pro-vaccine parent, but not always. “Family law is highly localized and very particular to the specific case,” she said. More often, courts hesitate to override a parent who, up until a divorce, has been a child’s primary decision-maker.
For all the years of Michael and Leah’s marriage, that person was Leah. When I spoke to her recently, I found her to be open about her beliefs. Her sincerity, combined with her slow Texas drawl, had an unembarrassed, guileless quality to it. She told me that, even if a medical cure for Donnie’s S.M.A. is never found, she hoped that “one day I can heal him from this.” Leah seemed to understand the turns in her life as twists of fate that had set her on a different “timeline.” “Whatever comes is meant to be,” she told me. She had not planned to become an anti-vaxxer, but she liked to keep an open mind; when arguments about the dangers of vaccines had arisen on the internet, she had accepted them into her way of viewing the world. If
MAHA
is a uniquely modern movement, born of fraying American systems, then Leah’s path reflected those same forces. She had sought community and identity online. Her experience of motherhood, the thing she valued most, had been transformed by pandemic-era fear and polarization. She had slipped away from the mainstream.
Leah was still waiting to hear whether Michael’s appeal would lead to a new family-court hearing. In the meantime, Donnie was scheduled to start public school in the fall. For a while, Michael believed that Leah would somehow try to circumvent the school’s vaccine requirements. At a recent pickup, he and Leah argued about one of the kids’ ear infections, while Michael, who was filming the interaction using a camera attached to his motorcycle, repeatedly asked, “Did you get Donnie set up for his vaccines for school?” He even considered taking Donnie to the doctor himself, without telling Leah. But, in August, Leah took the child to his first appointment. “It’s scary,” she told me afterward. “Anytime they get vaccines, or anything like that, I pray about it and make sure that they’re shielded in protection. That’s just the way I’m living.”
It was hard to imagine the two parents coming to an understanding. Michael was still frightened and disoriented by what had taken place over spring break. Whatever the kids had been sick with, he said, showed how risky this could be. “How are we going to make a sound decision if something goes crazy with Donnie?” he asked. To him, Leah had gone down a TikTok rabbit hole and never come out. “I feel like I’m living in crazy town,” he said on several occasions. Leah, for her part, had come to a serious, almost spiritual belief—reinforced by everything she saw online—in the fallenness of the medical establishment. How many well-meaning parents felt the same? It was clear to me that Leah, like the other
MAHA
moms I met, was motivated by a real desire to protect her children. This was something that even Michael could admit. “She loves her kids,” he said. “You can’t take that away from her.”
When I visited Michael in Charles Town, all three of his kids had made a full recovery, though problems remained: persistent ear infections, a stubborn case of dermatitis. Michael still had the hospital discharge papers in his truck. It was a Saturday, and I followed him and the children to a playground made up of two large play structures in a sea of wood mulch chips. No one else was there. Michael, who sometimes encouraged Donnie out of his chair to help him build muscle and independence, placed him in the mulch chips near the base of one of the structures, where Keith and Star were already climbing. The sun was blazing. “Get your hands the right way,” he called to Donnie, who was scooting through the wood chips. “Fists or palms, O.K.?”
At a nearby table, he took out his cigarettes and lit one up. In the spirit of free-range parenting, Michael told me, he believed in letting the kids wander. “Just go out and play and be kids,” he said. He wanted to teach them how to swim and take them camping. Across the playground, Star climbed to the top of a slide, then got too scared to come down. Michael retrieved her. Donnie seemed content on his own. I tried not to talk too much about the illness in front of the kids. Brianna had told me that they had been “terrified” to be so sick. Today, though, they seemed happy to be enjoying an aimless afternoon at Dad’s.
After a couple of hours, Keith ran over and asked when they were leaving.
He held up a small, bent twig like a weapon: “He’s a bad guy.
Pew
,
pew
,
pew
,
pew
.” He withdrew the twig, then said, “Now you’re a good guy.”
“Thank you,” Michael said.
Donnie was crawling over. Michael hoisted him up to the table with us. “I’m about to fall asleep,” Donnie said.
“O.K., lean on me here. You can sleep on me, O.K.?”
Star soon joined. “Meow,” she said.
The kids had already explored both play structures, said hi to a dog, and picked blades of grass beneath a tree. “Dad, when can we go home?” Donnie asked.
Michael loaded the children into the back seat and put Donnie’s wheelchair in the truck bed. “Star,” he said. “Seat belt, baby.” From the back seat, Star was asking for chicken nuggets, a treat that she associated with her father. Michael laughed. “Already?” he said. Star asked again. Michael said O.K. It was past lunchtime, anyway. They drove off to McDonald’s. ♦

epub_24.title: Lub Dub Lub Dub Lub Dub
epub_24.text:
Lub Dub Lub Dub Lub Dub
Fiction
Lub Dub Lub Dub Lub Dub
By Helen Simpson
August 30, 2026
“I wish I’d never read that piece about pacemakers,” Tracey said.
“You needed a new cooker, anyway,” Lois said. “You were saying your old one was about to give up the ghost.”
“How was I to know a plain electric hob would take forever to heat up?” Tracey fumed. “Then it gets too hot and it won’t turn down again and it burns everything. Disaster!”
“You did it for Adam,” Lois pointed out. “For his health.”
Read an interview with the author for the story behind the story.
Old friends, they were in one of London’s myriad Costas for a quick flat white before Lois’s 10:07 train from Euston. She was off on her fortnightly trek to the Midlands to visit her ninety-two-year-old mother.
A shriek of laughter from the gaggle of school mothers in the sofa area temporarily silenced them. The clack of cleated cycling shoes added to the din as three furry-legged men in helmets clattered up to the counter. The air was already at blood heat outside, and the men were sweating freely.
“How’s it been since Adam retired?” Lois asked.
Tracey thought about this. It had been the right time for him to stop. I prefer to call it “badinage,” he’d said when challenged about his workplace banter.
“Four Dyno-Rod callouts to the house in the past two weeks about our drains not working with maximum efficiency,” she said. “He’s off at the gym now. Which is ironic, as the gym’s the reason I’ve got to go to an effing three-hour workshop on cardiac arrests this morning.”
Podcast: The Writer’s Voice
Listen to Helen Simpson read “Lub Dub Lub Dub Lub Dub.”
Adam had been working out at the gym when the man on the running machine next to him had toppled off it while watching a replay of the previous night’s Champions League highlights. The gym’s defibrillator had blasted into action, and now the man was recovering from a triple bypass. “Only fifty-seven,” Adam had marvelled, shaking his head; he was sixty-five himself.
“Who knew an induction stovetop could mess with a pacemaker,” Lois said, reverting to their cooker conversation.
“Don’t get closer than two feet away or you might explode,” Tracey said. “You’ll need a mega-long wooden spoon to scramble your eggs if you’re going to risk it, according to that pesky health magazine.”
Adam’s father had had a pacemaker, like a little matchbox under his collarbone, and heart trouble was often genetic. Tracey was anticipating Adam’s need for one himself.
“It’s how
my
father went,” Lois said. “He didn’t really know anything about it—he’d been telling a funny story at the time, and he just stopped. That was it. So long ago now.”
His heart burst smilingly, Tracey thought, the shred of Shakespeare floating back across the decades. She’d done “King Lear” at school. Lately, all sorts of things she’d once read were reappearing.
“My mother’s been on her own now for well over thirty years,” Lois said. “She’s indestructible. I do worry about what’s going to happen, how it’ll end. She won’t have any help except from me, and her stairs are lethal.”
“Have you noticed, though,” Tracey said, “things don’t generally go as expected. Something happens out of the blue. Think of the Berlin Wall.”
“The Berlin Wall? I suppose so. Why didn’t you go for a gas stovetop, by the way?”
“Oh, I know. You don’t have to tell me. I love gas for cooking. So responsive! But apparently it’s the same as having a small car belching exhaust fumes into your kitchen, and Adam gets asthma now and then.”
“You can’t win, can you. Oh, look at the time! I’ve got to rush.”
The two women embraced briefly but warmly and set off on their different days.
At the workshop, in a local church hall, Tracey found herself sitting next to a woman who’d already done the course once and had come for a refresher. In the same week that this woman had first done it, she told Tracey, quite by chance she’d gone round to friends for dinner, and, just as their host was carrying in the fish pie, he’d dropped it and crashed to the ground with a heart attack. She was able to administer CPR right away, freshly primed with the relevant knowledge; no, he didn’t survive. It had made
her
feel better about it, though, having a go herself.
The course leader gave them her name at the start—Welsh for “snow,” she told them, a Celtic name that sounded to Tracey like “Weary,” although surely it couldn’t be that, even if it did suit her.
Lub dub lub dub lub dub is the noise of the heart beating when you listen with a stethoscope.
It’s a four-chambered pump ceaselessly squeezing the blood through your body, and its hundred thousand beats a day are powered by self-generated electrical impulses. A cardiologist clearly had to combine the skills of both plumber and electrician, Tracey thought as she listened to Weary’s account of what tended to go wrong.
Your heart’s supply pipes could get furred up. They could narrow right down and sometimes be completely blocked—then you would have to get stents or an ablation, and, if some really serious plumbing work needed to be done, the supply might be rerouted via some unblocked pipes borrowed from somewhere else. Often from your leg. Whereas when the electrics went wrong, when the rhythm of the pump fell out of kilter, a little generator, a pacemaker, could be wired in under the collarbone to put it right.
“When the heart stops for whatever reason,” Weary said, wearily, “whether it’s blocked arteries or electrical chaos, whatever—that’s what’s called cardiac arrest. After four minutes of no oxygen, the brain starts to die, but, if you keep the blood moving round the body with hefty chest compressions, you might gain a little more time.”
The workshop attendees shifted in their seats. Action at last.
“But, whatever you do, don’t try it if they’re breathing,” Weary added sternly. “Check if they’re breathing first.”
There was some uneasy laughter.
“I’ve seen relatives attempting to do CPR on someone while they’re trying to escape,” she continued, without smiling. “I’ve literally had to pull them off. So, how do you check? You check by getting your ear and cheek down close to their nose, their mouth, and feeling if there’s any breath coming out.”
Another scrap of Shakespeare appeared, longer this time, echoing down the corridor of memory. Lend me a looking glass; if that her breath will mist or stain the stone, Why, then she lives.
Tracey put her hand up.
“Would it work if you put a mirror to their mouth?” she asked.
“I have heard of that,” Weary said. “But, to be honest, most people don’t carry a mirror with them.”
More than ninety per cent of people who experience cardiac arrests outside of hospitals do not survive, they were told. Tracey stopped concentrating quite so hard when she heard this—what was the point?
A plastic torso and face was pulled from Weary’s rucksack. “Little Anne,” she said, tossing the demi-doll to the ground. With some effort, she got down onto her hands and knees to demonstrate how to do chest compressions.
“Arms straight. Push hard with your arms straight,” Weary said, “
and
release. Keep this up to the rhythm of ‘Stayin’ Alive,’ though you could go with ‘Baby Shark’ if you’re too young to know about the Bee Gees. We don’t advise ‘Nellie the Elephant’ anymore—it’s too slow.”
“How
hard
should you push?” the keen woman next to Tracey asked.
“
Pretty
hard,” Weary said. “Some think if you don’t break a rib, it’s not hard enough. I wouldn’t go so far as to say that, though, yes, I might well do some damage to the ribs, the cartilage. But if you don’t push down hard enough their brain will die.”
“Bloody hell,” Tracey muttered.
“To be honest, it’s very unlikely you’ll get that heart beating again without a defibrillator,” Weary said. “Which needs to be there within four minutes, ideally, if it’s going to work. So, as you can see, it’s
where
your cardiac arrest happens that matters most—I mean, at Heathrow you’d be O.K., or at the gym. But you might not be so lucky otherwise.”
I’d be useless, Tracey thought. We are enfleshed—that’s the mystery—but flesh is not all that we are. The body is important and interesting, but it’s not the whole story. Yes, when the heart stops beating, your light’s switched off. But until then . . .
Once home, hunched over a Nespresso, Tracey attended to the buildup on her iPhone, saving Lois’s WhatsApp voice note till last. Lois had had a falafel panini at the bus stop in Burton upon Trent, it seemed—not very nice but better than nothing—while waiting for the once-an-hour No. 9 to her mother’s flat in Ashby-de-la-Zouch. She was reporting in now from her childhood bedroom. Her mother was having a nap while she, Lois, sorted through her bills and medical appointments. She, Lois, was looking forward to a better night’s sleep, under her old candlewick bedspread, than she’d been managing recently; she was glad for her daughter that things were going well with the new boyfriend, but the walls were paper thin and she and William could hear everything; though, of course, she shouldn’t complain, it wasn’t her daughter’s fault that she couldn’t afford to move out at twenty-seven, and actually maybe she and William should think about downsizing, too, though they couldn’t really afford to either if they wanted to stay near London, where their life was.
Tracey’s voice note in response gave the morning’s workshop highlights, including the rib-cracking part, and she volunteered that she thought her—Lois’s—mother had been absolutely right to get her official D.N.R. statement framed and placed on the hall table, as otherwise any paramedics would be legally obliged to storm in and do goodness knows what, which seemed ridiculous. And, as for downsizing, she was just off now, as it happened, to view a flat with Ollie, the estate agent she’d told Lois about, the one who looked like Paul Mescal.
“It’s deceptively spacious,” Ollie said, as he always did.
“Um,” Tracey said.
They gazed together at the melancholy little room. It smelled dispiritingly stale. A fine pelt of dust coated the brown furniture; dust motes circulated sluggishly in the single ray of light struggling through the layer of window grime.
“Probate job,” Ollie added.
“Phew, it’s hot,” Tracey said, mopping her forehead with a tissue.
“Yeah, climate change, what can you do,” Ollie agreed. “I’m on leave next week, and it’ll be forty-three in Corfu! But that’s cool—I just want to chill by the pool.”
“Yes,” Tracey said.
Another heat wave was on the way, the second this year, and it was still only early May. Having lived in Britain all her life, Tracey’s thermostat was calibrated to milder days, and she didn’t do so well now that the outside air had started to exceed blood heat by several degrees on a regular basis.
That’s how they used to poach lobsters, she thought: alive, and slowly increasing the heat.
“How’s business?” she asked Ollie.
“Good, good,” he said earnestly, admiring his pointed brown shoes. Then he looked up at her and beamed. “They were saying at work, it’s already started, the cascade effect.”
“Cascade effect?” she asked, though she knew what it was. It was a phrase she kept hearing.
“Trillions!” he said with simple enthusiasm. “The greatest transfer of parent-to-child wealth in history, and all because of what’s happened to property prices.”
Tracey grunted her understanding of this.
“Our new sales initiative,” he said, laughing. “We call it Downsize and Die.”
Then he realized what he’d just said and blushed as red as a peony.
“Off the record,” he muttered, frowning down at his shoes this time.
“Of course,” Tracey said, soothingly.
At home, she smiled fondly at Downsize and Die, pausing to tap out a WhatsApp message to make Lois smile, too.
What was that piece of advice Ollie had given her last week, while he was showing her the basement flat on Harbinger Road?
“I always say, go with your gut, not with your heart,” he’d said mysteriously.
Go with your gut! Even as she was under sedation, the deep twisting sensation during her recent colonoscopy had made her groan. The long metal worm with its camera eye was like the one Dyno-Rod used on the drains. Adam didn’t yet know to leave well alone.
She turned back to the pile of novels she had been sorting through for Oxfam.
A sense of impending doom—that was how Weary had described the feeling many people got, like a heaviness in the chest.
It wasn’t as if you got to choose, though, Tracey mused, saving “In a Summer Season” and tossing “Under the Volcano” onto the giveaway pile.
Extraordinary that this Billy bookcase will outlive me, she thought. It’ll still be here years after I’ve gone.
Anyway, who cares? She’d had enough for one day. Death hath ten thousand several doors, get over it. Whichever way you go, it ends the same way. What would it profit me to be shot to death with diamonds or strangled with pearls? That wasn’t Shakespeare, was it? No, it was Webster.
Six o’clock. She turned the radio on. The slow chimes of Big Ben sounded, and then the newsreader’s solemn voice with the headlines.
Here was Adam at the door, back from his afternoon trip to the dentist.
She flicked off the radio and looked at him blankly.
“The world is run by awful old men,” she said.
“No debate there,” Adam said, unpacking some cans of beer from his man bag. “You won’t believe it when I tell you how much it’s going to cost for a root canal!”
His golden locks Time hath to silver turned. She was still getting used to the change in how he looked.
“I’m off to tennis in a minute,” he added.
“What,
again
?”
“
You
should take more exercise,” he said as he walked out of the room. “I don’t want you dying on me.”
“No,” she said.
“You know what I mean,” he said, putting his head round the door, then coming over to hug her. “I wouldn’t last long if you went. I’ll be having a drink with Pete afterward, by the way, so I’ll help myself from the fridge when I get back.”
“See you later,” she said.
Deciding that she’d have something from the freezer herself, she turned the oven on high to preheat. Good, there was an individual lasagna—just what she felt like. Tonight would be the first time she’d used the oven rather than the stovetop since the cooker’s arrival, last week, so this would be in the nature of a christening.
It certainly looked good, with the pasta’s bubbling béchamel clearly visible through the flawless glass door.
While she waited for her meal to heat through, she sat reading “In a Summer Season” at the kitchen table, enjoying the new oven’s industrious hum.
The next thing she knew, there had been a loud explosion.
Glass was everywhere—all over the table and floor, all over the kitchen, even caught in her clothes and hair.
“Bloody hell,” she said for the second time that day.
She waited for a moment before moving, and thought about it.
The oven must have blown up.
Yes, it was the oven door. It had burst into ten thousand diamond shards. It must have been made from some sort of tempered glass, she realized, for she wasn’t bleeding.
The lasagna was covered in glass jewels.
She crunched across the kitchen to fetch the oven’s manual. Nothing there.
She looked it up on her phone and, yes, how strange, oven doors did explode sometimes—it was a thing.
Not feeling quite ready to start clearing up yet, Tracey stood in the kitchen doorway and took a long, deep breath.
Then, while she waited for her heart rate to slow down, she WhatsApped her old friend Lois: “You’ll never guess what just happened.” ♦

epub_26.title: “The Disappearers” Stages the Pain and Pleasure of Jamaican Gay Life
epub_26.text:
“The Disappearers” Stages the Pain and Pleasure of Jamaican Gay Life
Books
“The Disappearers” Stages the Pain and Pleasure of Jamaican Gay Life
Marlon James’s new novel follows a group of gay men who seek love, connection, and restitution after a bloody homophobic attack.
By Katy Waldman
August 31, 2026
Marlon James’s novels, though they range from historical fiction to high fantasy, share a distinct spiritual frequency—a mix of bravado and bereavement. They are heroic in their scope, ambition, length, extremity, variety, unclassifiability, and apparent impulse to wrestle an entire world of external phenomena and internal experience between two covers. Yet this muchness tends to orbit a central absence. In James’s third book, “
A Brief History of Seven Killings
,” from 2014, a kaleidoscope of action and intrigue whirls around an artist known only as the Singer—a stand-in for Bob Marley—who departs from Kingston after an assassination attempt. The novel, a Talmudic compendium of multiplying, entangling plotlines, established James as a literary eminence, and made him the first Jamaican author to win the Booker Prize. In the wake of its success, he published two installments of a daring new project, a planned epic trilogy rooted in African mythology. James, invoking “
Game of Thrones
” as a touchstone, said that he’d been longing for “Black pageantry”; the works delivered verdant settings, Tarantino-esque blood spatter, and horseback riders in “flowing red robes, black armour, and gold crowns topped with feathers.” But all this manifold spectacle is triggered by a quest for a boy, possibly of royal lineage, who has gone missing. The first line of the first book seems to void everything that follows. “The child is dead,” the story begins. “There is nothing left to know.”
Does loss cancel out the life happening around it, or can life and loss coexist? James’s books are explicit and sensational, full of graphic depictions of sex and violence. There’s a sense of abundance and duplicity: the sprawling casts feature raving soliloquists, undercover agents, and tricksters who pepper their seductions with asides about literature and philosophy. James, who publicly came out as gay in his forties, after the publication of “A Brief History,” is alert to the spectrum of manliness—how aggression can give way to an unprotected softness, and how virile swagger can veer into camp. He glues together the pulpy and the delicate, seesawing at times between shock value and earned emotional devastation, playing with the cartoonish nature of our most intense experiences. In his newest book, “
The Disappearers
” (Riverhead), a son congratulates his father on probably being the first parent to wish that his child was raped in high school. The father offers, “What I shoulda done is kill you in your sleep.”
James is also evocative on the sentence level—in the same novel, a desolate character standing on a balcony hears a “little blue amoeba of pool” whispering to him from below. Phrases are turned a few degrees tighter than you’d expect from a writer who so rejects the cult of the single exquisitely resonant detail (why not a blizzard of details, some of which undermine one another?), and who has such an ear for speech. James’s dialogue fountains down the page, as if a tap has been opened. Life pours from him. There’s that vibrancy and, on the other side of the ledger, dead boys, ciphers, unfinished or unfinishable quests.
“The Disappearers” immediately showcases its author’s signature math of plenitude plus lack. It follows a group of gay men in Jamaica who seek love, connection, and restitution after a bloody homophobic attack. The explosion of malice effaces them in different ways, and James traces the mechanisms of their vanishing, examining how a person’s life can be compressed into smaller and smaller spaces. He seems preoccupied throughout by the simultaneity of having and losing. During a particularly ghastly scene, a character who’s dying of
AIDS
quotes “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner”: “Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink.” In its bleakest moments, the novel suggests that the ordeal of being gay in a venomously bigoted society negates its bounty.
Masculinity and its discontents are dominant themes for James, things that he’s explored with nuance and sensitivity in his almost etiological studies of violence. Gay desire has been more peripheral to his work, and is usually shadowed by danger. Queer characters filled out “Brief History” ’s taxonomy of social types, including Weeper, a ruthless enforcer and cocaine addict who slept with men in prison. Sent to oversee drug operations in New York City, Weeper discovers the East Village’s queer scene. It’s a netherworld of male-on-male hookups, adjacent to gangland and haunted by what one character calls “the gay cancer”—a veiled, subterranean setting that James uses to emphasize the mingling of invisibility, death, and pleasure.
If gay life and homophobia were once merely part of the Jamesian tapestry, “The Disappearers” puts these elements center stage. The book unfurls, playlike, in five acts. Each section has the feel of a dramatic monologue. James seems to be easing the reader in with Act I, a series of journal entries composed by the earnest, good-natured nineteen-year-old Eddy Porteous, who sees a coded flyer for a theatrical production and decides to audition. (It turns out that no auditions are necessary; just enough men have shown up for the director to cast the play.) The year is 1988, and the director, the stage manager, and the six performers offer a cross-section of that era’s gay life. Eddy hails from uptown; the director, Titus Havelock, was educated at Oxford; and the designated “top queen,” with blown-out hair and skin “smoother than the lotion he uses,” lives in a neighborhood where houses “look like shipping containers stacked together.” His name is Orrin, and he bears some resemblance to one of the main characters on “Get Millie Black,” from 2024, a Jamaican crime drama that James created for HBO.
The play that they will be staging is “Fortune and Men’s Eyes,” by the Canadian director John Herbert, about a community of incarcerated men. “Yes, there will be violence. Yes, there will be tenderness. Yes, there will be rape,” Havelock warns. Eddy, though, is more interested in his castmates, especially an acerbic college dropout and fellow comics connoisseur named Jordan Brown (“high, loose, curly hair . . . dimples”) and a guarded office worker who gives his name as Matt Chin. (“Brown. Tall. Half-Chinese-looking. Wide grin. Wow.”)
Eddy is a classic Nick Carraway bystander type, observant yet sweetly unaware of his magnetizing effect on the other characters. He’s stamped with the Jamesian trademarks of a smart mouth and pop-cultural fluency, dropping rat-a-tat references to Prince, Sinéad O’Connor, Bret Easton Ellis, “The Cosby Show,” and Bruce Springsteen (who owns “the biggest boss bulge in rock and roll”). Crucially, Eddy is also the only one of the players who can pass for white; when his journal entries end, so does the book’s innocence.
The chattiness of Eddy’s dispatches does little to conceal that the novel’s Jamaica is a grim place for gay men. A local university burns mattresses out of a fear of
AIDS
; even Eddy’s best girlfriend tosses off slurs. In the book’s second act, that malevolence erupts. A mob of men ambushes the players—minus Eddy, who isn’t there—at rehearsal, killing one actor and maiming the others. James roves among the attackers’ perspectives before and during the event, his experimental style, psychological acuity, and ragged lyricism on display. (“Lock yourself in a room let the dark and the heat boil you into a stew, let the heat go from fire in your skin to fire in your mind and blame that on them too blame them for even the dark.”) Also evident is the lurid hyper-violence that has occasionally caused critics to reach for words like “sadism” and “pornography” to describe James’s work. “I could make a charm bracelet out of all the teeth scattered on the floor,” one assailant jokes. A victim’s face acquires “two small wet holes that seem big like outer space; two bloody black holes where him eyes supposed to be.”
The rest of the book is aftermath. Upon being released from the hospital, two men disappear. Jordan, the dimpled college dropout, pursues vengeance, attempting to visit on the perpetrators of the assault what they instilled in him; James, as if stressing that the revenge plot constitutes its own gruesome genre, inflects Jordan’s story line with horror. For others in the cast, there’s respectable daytime Jamaica: church, work, loneliness. Havelock neither retreats to the closet nor holds out hope for resolution via vigilante justice. He moves into a hillside cottage—“the nearest neighbour is nearly a mile downhill”—and most days doesn’t “actually speak until the afternoon, if at all.” He reads, thinks, goes into town to earn a paycheck. “A quiet life,” he writes to a friend, before amending himself: “A sad life.”
In James’s hands, these branching options can seem to amount to distinctions without a difference. They appear to reflect the limitations of a world—Jamaica in the eighties—that disallows the happiness of gay people. Or Black gay people, at least. Eddy has been spared the worst violence; the novel casts his racial privilege as a kind of metaphysical exemption. The attack compounds his sense of exclusion, his already guilty conscience. Jordan, to whom scorn comes more naturally than grace, accuses him of envying the rest of the troupe’s ennobling misery. Do all Jamaican gay men, or possibly all nonwhite Jamaican gay men, have the same tragic story?
In the prison and in the play, “The Disappearers” finds two potent figures for gay life. The threat of the prison is that you’re targeted and unfree, packed into a queasy, pressurized intimacy with the most dangerous parts of yourself and others. The threat of the play is that you assume a role that obscures who you truly are. James, a sensitive diviner of both anxieties, chronicles how the inhospitality of the social world sends gay men into hiding. “We doing battyman hater work for them,” an elder observes. (“Battyman” is an offensive word for homosexual.) “Now it’s we who making sure we vanish.” What it means to collaborate in your own oppression—to use the master’s tools to add an annex to the master’s house—is a preoccupation for this author, who wrote, in “Brief History,” that “maybe is a ghetto thing where even if another man don’t destroy you, you going destroy yourself.”
But “The Disappearers” isn’t straightforwardly about self-contempt. Many of the characters don’t shun their homosexuality; rather, they see it as beautiful. Jordan says, in a kind of ecstasy, “I want to lick a nipple with thick hair around it, get my tongue stuck between two ass cheeks clamping down on it, shove my hand down either the front or the back of his pants and come away with the same funk, lick tobacco or mint off his tongue, inhale the breath that he snorts out like a bull, wrap my hands around his cock while he wraps around mine and we yank and pretend like it don’t hurt a little bit.” In James’s telling, a gay lover is a “bewitchment”; homosexual desire becomes a prison only when it causes you to be flattened and homogenized by suffering. During the cast’s first real rehearsal, the men struggle to articulate why they’re interested in theatre. One wants to feel brave, one wants to try something new, several seem defiant or to imply that they’re lonely. What they’re fumblingly vocalizing is a sense of possibility tied to the adoption of a new identity—a promise of self-creation that the mob manages to invert. Violence diminishes its victims, forcing everyone to play a single thankless role. “This attack,” Eddy tells Matt. “It changed you. It changed all of you.” When Matt points out that Eddy is stating the obvious, Eddy clarifies, “I mean it changed all of you into the same person.”
As the book proceeds, James blurs his actors together, in slightly eerie ways. Their stories aren’t interchangeable—some have endured a near-mythic amount of hardship, and others’ difficulties feel more ordinary—but the repetition underscores their commonalities: their repressive fathers, their chilly mothers, their vicious or bewildered classmates. Like James himself, the men are clever and bookish, writing letters or diaries, reading voraciously, and imagining themselves into tales of romance and Biblical comeuppance. They even speak one another’s lines. Matt lusts after “a runner whose living bulge bounces off one thigh then the other.” Jordan asks, in the middle of an ode to men’s bodies, “You ever watch a boy run, how everything flops on right thigh, then left?”
These overlapping, semi-porous characters search for one another, their paths intersecting. The questing and the keeping-tabs develop a mystical dimension; it’s as if the men have lost an incommunicable piece of themselves that they endlessly look for among their peers. Matt, whose perspective is largely withheld, remains the most enigmatic of the group, and the one most desperately sought after. James loans him elements of his own biography—memories and material that he’s talked about as part of his coming of age.
Still, the novel properly belongs to Jordan, a creation as canny and protean as the story itself. He’s a conflicted force of nature whose narration demonstrates James’s ability to execute rapid tonal shifts within paragraphs, to whipsaw into armored zingers from the heights of dreamy introspection. When Jordan first appears, during rehearsals, he comes off as self-protective, bright, and exasperating. After the attack, his witty, vulnerable voice holds together a chaotic and increasingly hallucinatory downward slide. He spies one of his attackers, a closeted man named Gareth, at a clandestine gay bar, and resolves to insinuate himself into his life, with the goal of eventually exposing him. The two start ambivalently sleeping together, and then dating each other. Throughout, terms like “anger” and “revenge” fail to express Jordan’s actual afflictions: the unbearable intimacies of identification, the ravages of sexual need. “Revenge never told me what revenge is supposed to be,” he says. “It just sits there like a fucking word.”
There’s a dark and delirious symmetry to the way Jordan and Gareth mirror each other’s self-hatred and desperate longing. The effect is claustrophobic, but, as with James’s other doublings, it’s also erotic, entrancing, and even freeing. The terror and the beauty of Jordan and Gareth’s assignations are that both men stop being able to tell themselves apart. Unsettlingly, the roles of victim and perpetrator bleed together. Who is seducing whom, and does it matter? Who is punishing, and who is being punished? These passages yield some of the book’s best writing. Likewise, James’s descriptions of cruising feel oddly creative, fluid, and primordial: at night, in a thicket of trees, it’s “all darkness and shadow and all touch and smell and taste,” Jordan thinks, and “a tongue is in my mouth before I say anything,” and “the hands refuse to stop grabbing, rubbing, and squeezing.” The fungibility of the hands is a reprieve from the book’s scenes of violence and its fallout, from the endless assigning of blame and the apportioning out of mercy or destruction.
In a tenderly melancholic moment, Jordan imagines a sexual encounter between two of his castmates—the novel’s tentative version of fulfillment. He pictures one of the boys thinking, mid-hookup, that “this shit is unreal” and seeking confirmation that “all of this is not some dream.” Of course, it is unreal, a play that Jordan is putting on in his mind. But it’s a play in which, unlike the larger drama that he and his fellow-actors have unwillingly been thrust into, the pain of being gay doesn’t nullify the pleasure. The role you inhabit can steal your future and imprison you in the past; it can also usher you into decent society at the cost of your soul (and it’s no accident that one of the narrowest closets in the novel turns out to be evangelical Christianity). But the permeability of James’s protagonists suggests that more than just these parts are possible. “The Disappearers” uses the tricks of fiction to pull off something extremely difficult: giving full weight to tragedy and injustice without implying that some lives are over before they’ve begun. ♦
