Has the Supreme Court Sandbagged Democracy?
A new legal history argues that the Justices should be stripped of their power to overrule coequal branches of government. It arrives at an awkward moment.
By Daniel Immerwahr
August 31, 2026
The liberal list of Republican offenses is long—so long, indeed, that the outrages blur. That time
Ted Cruz
shut down the government
for two weeks seems like a century ago, and, if anyone was ever angry about the White House promoting Melania Trump’s jewelry line, I can’t remember. One wound still festers, though: the Senate’s refusal in 2016 to consider Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominee, Merrick Garland.
Even before Obama named a candidate to fill the seat left vacant by Antonin Scalia’s sudden death, Republicans had announced their opposition. “Mr. President, you will not fill the Supreme Court vacancy,” Mitch McConnell, the Senate Majority Leader, declared. By nominating Garland, a moderate with admirers on both sides of the widening aisle, Obama offered Republicans a gamble: take Garland now or face whatever Pan-African, gender-free communist Hillary Clinton would summon from the judicial depths when she stepped into the Oval Office in 2017.
Republicans decided to risk it, insisting that eight months before an election was too soon to consider an outgoing President’s nominee. Blocking Garland helped their flailing candidate, Donald Trump. He boiled his pitch to hesitant conservatives down to two words, shouted at rallies: “Supreme Court.”
Supreme Court
. Trump lost the popular vote but won the election. Extraordinarily, this allowed him to appoint three Justices: Neil Gorsuch to fill Scalia’s seat, Brett Kavanaugh to fill that of the retiring Anthony Kennedy, and Amy Coney Barrett, whom Republicans rushed to confirm after Ruth Bader Ginsburg died, at eighty-seven, less than two months before the 2020 election. Trump increased his impact by selecting youthful appointees. If they last as long as Ginsburg did, the oldest, Kavanaugh, will serve through 2052, and the youngest, Barrett, until 2059. “No plausible definition of democracy makes this situation reasonable, let alone desirable,” Erwin Chemerinsky, the dean of U.C. Berkeley’s law school, has written.
Chemerinsky isn’t the first to gape at the Supreme Court’s undemocratic features. The Court is often described as “counter-majoritarian”; its composition doesn’t shift with the political winds. There’s an argument for this. Insulated from elections, Justices can guard against the frenzies that occasionally seize the voting public. Judicial power allows “Philip sober to control Philip drunk,” as Justice David Brewer famously put it in 1893.
Essentially, the Supreme Court is our democracy’s appointed buzzkill. In the early nineteen-thirties, it swatted down New Deal legislation passed by congressional majorities. In the fifties and sixties, it overturned segregationist laws enacted by state and local legislatures.
The Supreme Court is like ranked-choice voting or Jdate: how you feel about it depends on whether it’s delivering what you want. Which makes today’s situation confusing. A lawless President is asserting boundless authority, a Republican Congress is playing along, and it’s unclear, from case to case, where the Court will land. The Harvard law professor Cass R. Sunstein’s new book, “
Separation of Powers
” (M.I.T.), compares this state of affairs to the Nazi era and calls for a strong, independent judiciary. Trump won the popular vote; if there were ever a time for Philip sober to splash cold water on an inebriated majority, this would be it.
Except Philip is serving bottomless mimosas, the Court’s detractors claim. Yes, the Justices struck down Trump’s tariffs and preserved birthright citizenship. But they also gutted the Voting Rights Act, blocked federal remedies to fix extreme gerrymandering, permitted the President to fire commissioners of most regulatory bodies at will, and granted him broad immunity from criminal prosecution for acts undertaken in his official capacity. The last ruling, the three dissenting Justices have warned, “effectively creates a law-free zone around the President,” rendering him immune even if he “organizes a military coup” or “orders the Navy’s Seal Team 6 to assassinate a political rival.”
Two of Sunstein’s Harvard colleagues, Nikolas Bowie and Daphna Renan, take a different approach. In their formidable, sharply argued book, “
Supremacy
” (Norton), they distinguish two often conflated powers. The power of vertical review allows the Supreme Court to invalidate state and local laws that, in the Justices’ view, contradict federal ones. The power of horizontal review allows the Court to overrule a coequal branch of government and strike down federal laws or regulations. Few make this distinction today, but it reveals a pattern, Bowie and Renan contend: vertical review cuts both ways for liberal democracy, but horizontal review reliably serves regressive ends.
Most critics of judicial supremacy stumble over the fact that a strong Court sometimes benefits their side. Bowie and Renan, by identifying a consistently conservative power of the Court, vault that obstacle. Their case is then straightforward, albeit provocative: using horizontal review, the Supreme Court has sandbagged democracy. The thing needed, even in the days of galloping authoritarianism, is to cut the Court down to size.
Although the Supreme Court’s power to overrule Congress is now broadly accepted, it was bitterly contested for more than a century. Scholars have long known this, and Bowie and Renan’s book follows the tracks of important works like Larry D. Kramer’s “
The People Themselves
” (2004), Keith E. Whittington’s “
Political Foundations of Judicial Supremacy
” (2007), and Barry Friedman’s “
The Will of the People
” (2009). What Bowie and Renan add is that the loudest protests against horizontal review historically came from abolitionists, labor organizers, suffragists, and civil-rights activists.
As those critics noted, the Constitution doesn’t expressly authorize the Court to overturn acts of Congress. That right was supposedly established by Marbury v. Madison, in 1803. President John Adams, after losing his 1800 reëlection bid, used his lame-duck period to fill the judiciary with sympathizers. But some orders commissioning justices of the peace, though signed by Adams and sealed by his Secretary of State, went undelivered. The Court had to decide whether Thomas Jefferson’s Administration could be forced to turn them over, under the Judiciary Act of 1789.
It was a bizarre case, reflecting the era’s anything-goes atmosphere. John Marshall, the Chief Justice, had been the Secretary of State who’d sealed those commissions and been responsible for their delivery. Jefferson, his cousin, tried to block the case by signing a federal law that prevented the Court from meeting for fourteen months. Marshall then used Marbury v. Madison to proclaim the Court’s ability to invalidate federal laws that it deemed unconstitutional. Bowie and Renan point out that Marshall (perhaps intentionally) misread the statute that he was invalidating, making the whole thing a turducken of judicial folly.
Because the Court lacked a permanent abode, Marshall read out the ruling from the steps outside Stelle’s Hotel, on Capitol Hill. As with most impassioned avowals made on hotel steps, Congress ignored it. The Marbury decision didn’t compel anyone to do anything, so Marshall’s assertion just hung in the air.
Judicial assertions meant less back then. In ways that are hard to conceive of now, early-nineteenth-century politicians simply defied the Court. States regularly declined to appear before it when ordered. “Virginia’s highest court refused to concede that the Supreme Court had the authority to review its decisions,” Friedman writes. “Georgia actually hanged a man in the face of a Supreme Court order to the contrary.”
Within this rowdy milieu, there was nonetheless a growing constituency for “Philip sober” guardrails. The most eloquent plea for protections against zealous majorities came from the South Carolina statesman John C. Calhoun. His “
Disquisition on Government
,” published posthumously, in 1851, captured the view of the imperilled minority to which Calhoun himself belonged: slaveholders.
It is, of course, Noah’s-flood-on-your-wedding-day ironic that slaveholders would see themselves as oppressed. But a population boom in the North and the mainstreaming of antislavery politics there raised the threat of a legislative majority abolishing their property. Passions ran especially hot over slavery in the territories, where federal law held sway. The President elected in 1856, James Buchanan, swore that the “great object” of his Administration would be “to arrest, if possible, the agitation of the slavery question.” Buchanan secretly pressed the Court to take the divisive issue out of politicians’ hands. The Chief Justice, Roger B. Taney, obliged. In Dred Scott v. Sandford, his Court held that Black people lacked U.S. citizenship and that congressional bans on territorial slavery were unconstitutional.
Dred Scott, decided in 1857, was the Court’s first use of horizontal review since Marbury and its first substantial use of the power ever. It is widely regarded as the Court’s worst decision—a “hell-black judgment,” the abolitionist Frederick Douglass called it. But Douglass didn’t take Dred Scott as settled law; he took it as an invitation to challenge the Court’s authority. Outrage at Taney’s power grab filled the sails of the antislavery Republican Party and ultimately propelled Abraham Lincoln to the Presidency. In his Inaugural Address of 1861, he declared that permitting robed Justices to settle major disputes would mean that “the people will have ceased to be their own rulers.”
And so, like many before him, Lincoln defied the Court. After eleven slaveholding states seceded to form the Confederacy, Republican lawmakers passed and Lincoln signed a bill that flouted Dred Scott by prohibiting slavery in the territories. Bowie and Renan view this as a heartening reminder that the elected branches of government needn’t defer to the judiciary.
Taney remained Chief Justice until 1864, when he died. During the Civil War, he watched impotently as the Lincoln Administration brushed off rulings on habeas corpus, Black citizenship, and, of course, slavery. “There was no sadder figure to be seen in Washington,” the journalist E. V. Smalley wrote. “He had outlived his epoch, and was shunned and hated by the men of the new time.”
The reign of Republicans during the Civil War and Reconstruction was a democratic breakthrough in two senses. First, legislative majorities overrode the Court, repeatedly ignoring its rulings and adjusting the number of Justices to prevent its interference. Second, those majorities abolished slavery, extended citizenship, and guaranteed equal protection to all Americans. The historian Eric Foner, in “
The Second Founding
” (2019), describes this as the country’s “first attempt, flawed but truly remarkable for its time, to build an egalitarian society on the ashes of slavery.”
The Court struck back. Toward the end of Reconstruction, it began regularly overturning federal legislation. “By the end of the century, the Supreme Court undid nearly every major law Congress passed to protect multiracial democracy in the South,” Bowie and Renan write. It then turned to opposing labor unions, farmers’ organizations, and capitalism’s other foes.
This was the context for Justice Brewer’s remarks about Philip sober restraining Philip drunk. Judicial sobriety, for Brewer, meant protecting the respectable white man from “the anarchist, the socialist, and every other assassin of liberty.” The “eager and earnest protest of the Anglo-Saxon” was for “individual freedom and absolute protection of all his rights of person and property,” Brewer explained, in 1893. Two years later, he joined a majority in finding the federal income tax unconstitutional. (It would take a constitutional amendment to restore the government’s power to tax incomes.)
Between 1890 and 1936, using both horizontal and vertical review, the Court invalidated more than two hundred progressive statutes, state and federal. Historians call this the Lochner era, for Lochner v. New York, a 1905 case holding that a New York law limiting working hours violated the Fourteenth Amendment. In a characteristic turn, the Justices redeployed protections intended for Black citizens to benefit business owners.
Even establishment politicians like Teddy Roosevelt balked. He proposed allowing voters to overturn judicial decisions by ballot. If the spirit of Lochner were to prevail, he warned, “we should not only have a revolution, but it would be absolutely necessary to have a revolution.”
Such mutinous talk only heightened conservative Justices’ sense that the barbarians were storming the gate. “I must stay on the court in order to prevent the Bolsheviki from getting control,” Chief Justice William Howard Taft wrote to his brother, in 1929. As President, Taft had blocked Arizona and New Mexico’s joint bid for statehood because Arizona’s proposed constitution would have allowed voters to recall judges. As Chief Justice, he persuaded Congress to move the Court from its rooms within the Capitol to a dedicated marble edifice with bronze doors weighing six and a half tons apiece.
It was a “magnificent structure,” the columnist Howard Brubaker remarked upon its opening, with “fine big windows to throw the New Deal out of.” Indeed, after Democrats won the Presidency, the House, and the Senate in 1932, the largely Republican-appointed Supreme Court stood as a citadel of laissez-faire capitalism against the national zeal for economic controls.
The familiar understanding is that F.D.R. subdued the conservative Justices by threatening to enlarge the bench and swamp it with his appointees. This is a myth; they started to yield before he made that threat. And, in a way, the standoff reflected the judiciary’s growing authority. Unlike its nineteenth-century critics, F.D.R. had implicitly accepted horizontal review; his challenge had been to the Court’s orientation, not its powers. Once that orientation changed, the marble-ensconced Court was supremer than ever.
By the time F.D.R. died, in 1945, he had appointed seven of the Supreme Court’s nine Justices. This inaugurated a golden age of liberalism and a break with the Court’s theretofore conservative history. When Earl Warren presided, from 1953 to 1969, the Court helped make voting fairer, establish rights for criminal defendants, and dismantle Jim Crow. The Warren Court’s watershed decision of 1954, Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, which rejected segregation in public schools, is revered with the same intensity that Dred Scott is reviled.
Brown was a moment of both moral clarity and jurisprudential mystification, Bowie and Renan maintain. The lawyers for the plaintiffs, including the future Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall, had grounded their argument partly in a Reconstruction-era federal statute, the Ku Klux Klan Act. The case could be understood, then, as a straightforward matter of striking down state laws that violated a national one. It’s far from clear that the Court saw it this way, though; its unanimous opinion didn’t mention the Klan Act. Bowie and Renan lament the omission. Although the Court was, in their view, merely enforcing Congress’s will, it “gave the impression, whether intentionally or not, that it was acting alone, regardless of what Congress wanted.”
This is a crucial plank in Bowie and Renan’s argument. A Supreme Court lacking the power of horizontal review could still have issued the Brown decision. Most of the Warren Court’s admirable activism, they say, was in fact vertical review, targeting state and local statutes. They are correct. Of the twenty-four landmark Warren Court decisions listed by the legal website
Justia
, none overturned an act of Congress. If the Warren Justices had a bone to pick with legislators, it was with the state and local ones upholding Jim Crow.
To be sure, overturning a federal law is rare during any era of the Court. The Justices’ daily business involves resolving ambiguities, clarifying jurisdiction, harmonizing conflicting statutes, and adjudicating conflicts in special jurisdictions. And of the 1,514 laws that the Supreme Court struck down from its inception to mid-2017, only a hundred and eighty-two of them—twelve per cent—were federal. The Warren Court’s relative respect for federal laws was thus noticeable but not startling.
Although there haven’t been many federal invalidations, Bowie and Renan rightly observe that they account for some of the most regrettable decisions in Supreme Court history. In horizontal-review mode, the Court has struck down laws limiting slavery and child labor, establishing income taxes and minimum wages, and restricting corporations from tilting elections or firing workers for union activity. Horizontal-review success stories include invalidating the part of the Defense of Marriage Act defining marriage as exclusively between a man and a woman; few others come to mind. The triumphs are “dwarfed” by the “vastly larger” set of disasters, Bowie and Renan write.
The Warren Court had little need for horizontal review, Bowie and Renan believe, but it clung to that power nonetheless. A decision mandating school desegregation in Little Rock, Arkansas—signed by every Justice, for boldface emphasis—insisted that the Court’s supremacy over the other branches in interpreting the Constitution had been accepted since Marbury as “permanent and indispensable.” As history, this was ludicrous. The Warren Court, while making substantively democratic rulings, cemented a procedurally undemocratic arrangement.
Yet it was hard to mind back then. This was the heroic era of “
12 Angry Men
,” “
Inherit the Wind
,” and “
To Kill a Mockingbird
,” of principled men defending the law against racists and religious zealots. The Court seemed noble to progressives—maybe even cool. In 1970, Warren, recently retired, addressed a packed quad at the University of California, San Diego. The school had been roiled by protests, so when students unfurled a banner Warren’s supporters feared the worst. But the banner said “Right On, Big Earl!” and the crowd roared.
In gratifying the left, the Warren Court debilitated the long tradition of opposing judicial supremacy. Just how debilitated it was became clear in the deadlocked Presidential contest between George W. Bush and Al Gore. In a similarly close nineteenth-century election, between Rutherford B. Hayes and Samuel J. Tilden, Congress had taken charge and no one had “ever dreamed of trying to resolve it in litigation,” Larry D. Kramer notes. Yet, in 2000, the dispute went through the judiciary as a matter of course. After the Supreme Court decided for Bush, who’d lost the popular vote, Democrats acquiesced. “While I strongly disagree with the Court’s decision, I accept it,” Gore said, adding that the process had shown the “strength of American democracy.”
Late-twentieth-century politicians had grown comfortable with the Court’s authority. They could accept a view of politics as a turn-based game: the checks that they abhorred when they were in power, like horizontal review and the filibuster, became crucial when they were out. Counter-majoritarian arrangements insured that democracy didn’t devolve into two parties taking turns tyrannizing each other.
Democrats, with their signature concern for minority rights, had additional reasons to distrust straightforward majority rule. The legal theorist Lani Guinier argued in the nineteen-nineties that winner-take-all elections endangered Black individuals like her, who made up only ten per cent of voters. Thinking along the lines that John C. Calhoun once had, she considered alternative voting systems that could guard against “the tyranny of the majority.” Guinier’s more exotic ideas stirred controversy. (“Loony Lani,” right-wingers called her, among other things.) But she argued that minority protections made intuitive sense. She noted that her four-year-old son, Niko, had spontaneously proposed some when adjudicating which game a group of children should play.
That four-year-old, Nikolas Bowie, is now a Harvard law professor and in a different mood. His book with Daphna Renan vigorously defends majority rule against institutional impediments. The two authors cling to Congress, which they deem “more democratic than the Supreme Court.” For all its flaws, it “
is
our institution for translating the people’s power into enacted law.”
Bowie and Renan’s view fits a growing liberal discontent with the Court, no doubt stemming from Democrats’ recent failures to fill its seats. In principle, the Supreme Court supplies general drag, forcing whichever party is in power to contend with Justices appointed by previous Administrations. But the friction coefficient is now far greater in one direction. In the span of the Presidencies that yielded today’s Court, Republicans won the popular vote less than a third of the time but have appointed two-thirds of the current Justices.
In the first half of Joe Biden’s Presidency, Democrats controlled the White House and Congress yet faced a conservative Court, thanks partly to the Merrick Garland mishegoss. This was the exasperating moment when Bowie and Renan started publishing their critique of judicial supremacy and their demand to “reclaim the authority of Congress.” Biden called for reforms, too, in his final year, recommending that the Court’s Justices be limited to eighteen-year terms, staggered so that Presidents could appoint one every two years.
The Republican House Speaker, Mike Johnson, declared Biden’s proposal “dead on arrival.” Certainly, Biden’s planned announcement of his Court-reform scheme was drowned out by his less planned announcement, the same month, of his withdrawal from the 2024 Presidential race. At that point, Biden’s talk of mandatory retirement for aging officeholders hit awfully close to home.
Bowie and Renan want elected officials to reassert their authority over appointed Justices. Although the model they point to is Republicans in the eighteen-sixties, the most prominent case of this today is Israel. Its Supreme Court has rejected draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews and overturned a law legalizing settler homes built on private Palestinian land. That, in turn, has led Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing parliamentary majority to announce
plans to overhaul the judiciary
, including removing its horizontal-review power. (Unsurprisingly, the Supreme Court has struck down a law that would have constrained its ability to strike down laws.) Netanyahu’s allies present their ongoing judicial-reform campaign as a defense of the popular will.
Donald Trump shares Netanyahu’s impatience with meddling judges. Whereas his recent predecessors groused about the Supreme Court’s decisions yet acknowledged its larger usefulness, Trump, a
YOLO
President, is ready to napalm whatever obstructs his immediate interests. After the Court gave his birthright-citizenship executive order a skeptical hearing, he blasted his own appointees as “fools and lap dogs” and threatened to “PACK THE COURT!” Trump’s Vice-President, J. D. Vance, has warned of an “effort by the courts to quite literally overturn the will of the American people.” He’s admonished the Supreme Court to be “extremely deferential” to decisions “made by the people’s elected President.”
Trump and Vance worry that the Supreme Court will thwart executive actions. Although Congress doesn’t pass many laws these days, the White House has been a furious tempest of executive orders. And so the judicial battleground today isn’t between the Court and Congress but between the Court and the Presidency.
The Supreme Court’s self-granted power to declare executive actions unconstitutional hardly appears in Bowie and Renan’s history. But it’s hard to see how this power could be legitimate by their logic. If the Court is trammelling democracy when it overturns acts of Congress, isn’t it doing the same when it overrules a popularly elected President?
Bowie and Renan’s book, imploring politicians to defy the Court and obey the people, would have fit a Kamala Harris Administration perfectly. Trump’s reëlection, however, makes their “popular will versus injustice” framing harder to nod along with. Democrats could once take comfort in the notion that theirs was the popular side, with only the vagaries of the Electoral College and the iniquities of corporate campaign donations preventing them from permanently occupying the Oval Office. Yet in 2024 Trump, despite being significantly outspent, not only won the popular vote but did especially well with the working class. If the people had a will in that election, it was for deportations, tariffs, and cage matches on the South Lawn.
The Supreme Court has been a fitful friend to Trump in his second term, alternately enabling and impeding him. Much of its aid has come in unsigned rulings on the emergency docket—ostensibly temporary and non-precedent-setting judgments that nevertheless carry serious consequences. Horizontal review hasn’t yet seen much play. But, given that the Republicans now control both houses of Congress and the Presidency, curbing Trump might require firing that torpedo.
Bowie and Renan’s compelling history doesn’t lead one to expect much there. The Court has been persistently reactionary in its dealings with other branches, using horizontal review to protect enslavers from abolitionists, bosses from unions, and tycoons from tax collectors. Justice would have been better served, historically, by the Justices butting out.
Still, is now the time to desupremify the Court? Trump has been losing both support and inhibition. He’s likely to turn desperate as he finishes his second term, and he has threatened to seek a third. This is precisely the scenario that defenders of judicial supremacy have long warned about: Philip on a drunken rampage.
It is, as the grocers say, a pickle. Philip sober has been no friend to democracy. These days, though, he might be its best hope. ♦

epub_28.text:
Briefly Noted
Books
Briefly Noted
“The Black Shield,” “Endless Endings,” “Solstice,” and “I Was Bonnie & Clyde.”
August 31, 2026
The Black Shield
, by Wilbert L. Cooper (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)
. In this multilayered work, a journalist examines a Black police organization, known as the Black Shield, that emerged in Cleveland in the nineteen-forties, alongside his own parents’ membership in it. Cooper assesses the notion that Black communities are “safer and served better” when the police who surveil and discipline them are Black, too. In theory, he writes, the Black Shield offers opportunity for young people living in the economically distressed community where it is based, but he concludes that the group is less focussed on justice than on “getting the same lack of accountability that White officers enjoyed.” His ultimate indictment is nuanced, and has shades of appreciation—for his parents, and for the badge that “shielded my family.”
Endless Endings
, by Ricard Solé, translated from the Spanish by Eduardo Aparicio (Princeton)
. A single cell serves as the starting point for this lyrical exploration of death. From a consideration of apoptosis—the orderly elimination of damaged or unnecessary cells—Solé moves on to failing machines, eroded memories, vanished languages, brittle digital archives, and more. His overarching idea is that organisms, minds, technologies, and cultures survive by sustaining flows of matter, energy, or information; their final deaths occur not when a single constituent part disappears but when the processes holding the larger system together falter. Solé reveals a paradox: death is not merely life’s opposite but also one of its organizing forces, a constant cycle of removal and renewal through which complex systems are preserved.
What We’re Reading
Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.
Solstice
, by Carol Gilligan (Random House)
. This tender novel of intimacy and its risks begins in Boston in 1969, as Eve, a dancer, commences an affair with a colleague—an indiscretion that spurs her husband, a journalist named Gabe, to cheat, too. Under the influence of their era’s changing sexual mores, they soon reconcile. But then, in the eighties, Gabe returns from a reporting trip to the Middle East having taken up with a much younger woman. By this time, the couple share decades of history, along with three children. Gilligan’s portrait of their relationship is a study of how time binds people together. “There was a membrane now stretching between them,” she writes, “encompassing the two of them and enclosing them, fragile and yet impermeable.”
I Was Bonnie & Clyde
, by Laura Kasischke (Copper Canyon)
. The wily, beguiling poems in this collection probe selves and stories as sites of rupture and refraction. The book’s eponymous poem, for instance, begins, “You were Friday & Death. / I was Jekyll & Hyde. / You were my mother. / I Alive.” Throughout, Kasischke’s images ricochet off one another—suggesting narrative while resisting its confines, evoking stereotypical ideas and expectations of Western womanhood only to upend them. In a voice at once biting and contemplative, eerie and funny, Kasischke crafts poems in which nothing is ever stable or resolved. There is only “The confusion of the past / as fireproof as ash. // The follies of the future / as bulletproof as water.”

epub_29.title: Who’s Afraid of A.I. Music?
epub_29.text:
Who’s Afraid of A.I. Music?
Pop Music
Who’s Afraid of A.I. Music?
When the rapper Fenix Flexin débuted a new accent on his single “Rubberz,” he stumbled into a century-old fight over musical fraudulence.
By Kelefa Sanneh
August 31, 2026
Earlier this summer, a small night club in Passaic, New Jersey, hosted a brief performance by one of the year’s most talked-about musicians. A post on Instagram had promised attendees “an unforgettable night,” although not necessarily a long one: the only assurance was that the Los Angeles rapper known as Fenix Flexin would be “performing his viral hit ‘Rubberz’ live!” Until recently, Fenix was known for high-spirited and slightly mush-mouthed hip-hop tracks, but “Rubberz,” which was released in June, marked a dramatic change: it was sad but sprightly synth pop, like an unheard outtake from the nineteen-eighties; the vocals were crisp, with a hint of vibrato and a faintly British accent. Listeners seemed to delight in the incongruity—a semipopular rapper suddenly sounded nothing like himself.
Plenty of people thought they knew why. They guessed that the song had been created with artificial intelligence, which makes it trivially easy to generate a realistic song using nothing more than a brief description. Perhaps the voice on the track didn’t belong to Fenix, or, in fact, to anyone at all. The rapper appeared to deny this. When the YouTube journalist Andrew Callaghan asked Fenix whether he wanted to clear up misconceptions about “Rubberz,” he declined. “Oh, like the A.I. shit?” he said. “Nah. Shit is recorded like any other song.” He also sang some of the words for Callaghan, although neither the sound of his voice nor the lyrics he delivered were an exact match. “The watch is getting quicker,” he crooned; on the recording, it’s “The watch is
moving
quicker.”
On this night in New Jersey, no one seemed inclined to conduct a forensic investigation into the authenticity of the song, which Fenix performed twice, singing along with a prerecorded version of it and reproducing the slightly weird pronunciation: “Mon
ey
talk is much louder now,” he sang, stressing the second syllable in the line. “Hatin’ that I’m able,” he sang, pronouncing the sharp “t” in the first word, rather than softening or eliding it, the way most Americans would. He even did a few lines a cappella, which might have been a message to the doubters, or else a concession to tradition: suffice it to say that Fenix Flexin is not the first rapper to find himself in a night club, at 1
A.M.
, performing a notably imprecise rendition of his own hit single.
All summer long, as “Rubberz” was becoming harder to ignore, so, too, were questions about A.I. in music. When Kanye West released the album “Bully,” in March, fans tried to figure out whether certain tracks had been created with A.I., a technology West had previously praised. (West was later sued by a producer who claimed he had helped the artist create A.I. vocals on “Bully” and its predecessor, “Vultures II.”) Startups including Suno allow users to create songs partly or wholly powered by A.I., and some A.I. entities have begun to attract followings: Eddie Dalton, an old-school soul singer who corresponds to no physical human being that we know of, has half a million monthly listeners on Spotify—about as many as Clarence Carter, who died in May, at the age of ninety. In June, an Australian producer and d.j. named Josh Fawaz made it to No. 4 on the
Billboard
Hot Dance / Electronic Songs chart with an A.I. version of “Like a Prayer.” And HUGEL, a popular French d.j. and producer, has one of the summer’s biggest dance hits with “Movin’ to the Sun,” which seems to be a remix of an A.I. track that was originally associated with a social-media account said to belong to a Reiki healer from Hungary known as Imael Angel. The new version is jointly credited to HUGEL, Imael Angel, and the legendary house-music singer Ultra Naté, who apparently lent her human voice to this transhuman collaboration.
It would be an understatement to say that the growing prominence of A.I. music is generating backlash—sometimes it seems this music generates nothing
but
backlash. A producer named Medasin made a video arguing, convincingly, that Fenix and his collaborator Purps on the Beat had used an A.I. program called Treblo to make “Rubberz,” and he showed how easy the process might have been. (Using simple prompts such as “synthwave 80s” and “lyrics that are resemblant of a rapper lifestyle,” Medasin got the app to spit out a distinctly “Rubberz”-like song.) Afterward, Fenix changed his story. “Never said I didn’t use AI,” he wrote on Instagram, adding, “ain’t nothing wrong w using new technology as a tool keep up w the times or get left behind.” When a puckish British electronic duo known as Two Shell talked, in a recent interview, about using A.I., Tom Breihan, a senior editor for the music site
Stereogum
, delivered an unambiguous verdict that summed up the general mood: “No! Wack! Fuck that shit!” A month ago, a rapper named Tyga released a synth-pop album of his own, and he spoke freely about using A.I. to make it. His reward was a score of 0.0 from
Pitchfork
(the site’s first zero rating in nearly twenty years), and a similarly harsh review from the pop star Doja Cat: “Tyga is a penis for making an A.I. album.”
Sometimes this backlash concerns the ethical implications of A.I., which produces music by drawing from preëxisting songs, often without compensating the humans who made them. (“I feel like I’m at war because of A.I.,” the singer SZA said, in a recent interview.) But even more people seem concerned about the way A.I. lowers the barriers to musical entry, allowing would-be musicians to skip the step where they learn a skill or express a feeling. Many listeners—and not a few musicians—regard the process of making a song with A.I. as not just uncreative but anti-creative, and maybe anti-human, too. Earlier this year, the musician and producer Jack Antonoff posted a brief manifesto online, which said, “To everyone who is gassed up about the new ways you can fake making art, by all means drive right off that cliff.” To Antonoff and others, A.I. music seems neither good nor bad but something else altogether: fraudulent.
The fight against musical fraudulence has a long and illustrious history. The current battle dates at least to 1906, when John Philip Sousa testified before the House Committee on Patents. Sousa, who wrote military marches such as “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” was perhaps the most popular composer America ever produced, and he had come to deliver a warning. “These talking machines are going to ruin the artistic development of music in this country,” he said, of a device that was a few decades old and growing in popularity—the phonograph. In an essay published the same year, Sousa referred to phonographic cylinders and disks as “canned music,” a degraded form that could never, he said, capture or transmit the qualities that make music special. “Music teaches all that is beautiful in this world,” Sousa wrote. “Let us not hamper it with a machine that tells the story day by day, without variation, without soul, barren of the joy, the passion, the ardor that is the inheritance of man alone.” Sousa’s concern was not entirely aesthetic: part of his complaint about what he called “infernal machines” was that phonograph manufacturers paid no royalties to composers; his testimony helped inspire the 1909 Copyright Act, which changed that. In 1930, when theatres were replacing live orchestras with prerecorded soundtracks, the American Federation of Musicians launched a new campaign against “canned music,” buying a series of newspaper advertisements to decry the “corruption of an art by soulless mechanization.” One image depicted a man playing guitar flanked by a robot playing a banjo, and the text made an argument that many A.I. skeptics repeat today: “Where there is no feeling, no emotional capacity, there can be no music.”
Of course, this canned music was composed and performed by humans; “mechanization” referred only to the technology that allowed the performances to be recorded and played back. Aldous Huxley, in his novel “Brave New World,” from 1932, imagined, instead, a “synthetic music machine” able to autonomously create an endless soundtrack; around the same time, a company called Muzak was commissioning instrumental recordings that it delivered, via telephone wire, to workplaces and homes, creating a non-stop stream of background music. (In this magazine, in 1947, a Muzak executive described his product as “music you can eat to, shave to, work to, but not listen to.”) Muzak was a corporate success, although it swiftly became a cultural punch line—people used “Muzak” as a pejorative term for anything dull and low-quality. Starting in the eighties, the company began to supplement its library with original recordings of popular songs: a slightly less canned version of canned music. The company abandoned the name Muzak in 2013, by which time most of us had long stopped noticing the omnipresence of background music in our daily lives. Sousa was wrong to imagine that America might be able to resist the lure of the phonographic disk and its successors, but he was right to imagine that the recording industry would transform our ideas about what music is, while more or less killing off the tradition of the after-dinner sing-along and all but eliminating pianos from the nation’s living rooms. In popular music especially, the authentic artifact is now the recording, while a live performance is typically an ancillary experience.
As recording studios became more sophisticated, and more central to popular music, artists occasionally sought to reassure fans that they were really hearing what they thought they were hearing. The self-titled début album from the band Queen, from 1973, included in its instrumental credits a stern disclaimer: “ . . . and nobody played synthesizer.” The rock band Boston issued a similar statement (“No Synthesizers Used”) in a 1978 album, and so did Rage Against the Machine in 1992 (“
NO SAMPLES, KEYBOARDS OR SYNTHESIZERS USED IN THE MAKING OF THIS RECORDING
”), and the White Stripes in 2003 (“No computers were used during the writing, recording, mixing or mastering of this record”). By contrast, Stevie Wonder seemed proud to tell listeners that his 1972 album, “Music of My Mind,” contained both Moog and
ARP
synthesizers, which were then a novelty. He emphasized that his album was “virtually the work of one man”; technology was making it easier for musicians to work alone, helping them to create records that could be touted as
more
personal. Many pioneers of electronic pop acknowledged this tension by making music that was self-consciously robotic, like Kraftwerk paying tribute to “the man-machine” or Ultravox singing, deadpan, “I want to be a machine.” And yet these synth-pop musicians were nevertheless eager to insist that their music was
real
music. In a documentary about the synthesizer era, Andy McCluskey, from the English electronic-pop group Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, described his creations in terms Sousa might have appreciated: “It was all written by real human beings, and it was all played by hand.”
It may be no coincidence that “Rubberz” drew inspiration from this period in particular. (It sounds a little bit like “If You Leave,” an O.M.D. hit from 1986.) The song is a pastiche of a form of musical innovation that now sounds quaint, precisely because of its perceptible artificiality; the sharp backbeat and arpeggiated synthesizers remind us of an earlier and perhaps simpler time. By the end of the eighties, discussions of musical authenticity usually centered on the use of prerecorded sounds. In hip-hop and other genres, producers were using snippets of other people’s records; courts often ruled that this was a form of theft, although hip-hop fans tended to see it as righteous theft. And, onstage, pop musicians frequently performed alongside recorded tracks, which audiences tolerated—to a point. In 1990, the German duo Milli Vanilli was exposed for having lip-synched both onstage and, in effect, on record, as the two ostensible members of the duo had nothing to do with its music. This, everyone seemed to agree, crossed a line; the group eventually disbanded, and in the aftermath of the scandal the state of New Hampshire passed a law requiring concert promoters to inform audiences when they know, in advance, that “all the lead vocals consist of played recordings rather than the actual singing of those vocalists.” (New York recently enacted a similar law, aimed at A.I., requiring companies to notify the public if advertisements feature “synthetic performers,” although this law explicitly excludes movies and other “expressive works”—presumably including songs.) Nowadays, most big concerts include at least some prerecorded elements; one duty of a touring drummer is to play in time with a click track, which keeps the music onstage in synch with the music on tape. Since so much modern popular music consists of electronic elements, it’s not always clear what it might mean to play these songs “live.” Often, what a concert offers is the undeniable thrill of being in the same room as the person who made the music, regardless of the precise meaning of “made.”
Museumgoers generally agree that a great artist need not wield a paintbrush. They understand that some celebrated artists have assistants, or studios full of them, while others incorporate found or readymade objects into their practices; indeed, the word “practice” encourages viewers to think holistically about the creative process, instead of fixating on the final product. Avant-garde composers have sometimes built work out of noise or silence, or they’ve written scores that consisted only of instructions, some of which may remind contemporary audiences of A.I. prompts. (La Monte Young, “Composition 1960 #13”: “The performer should prepare any composition and then perform it as well as he can.”) In the world of popular music, different genres tend to have slightly different rules. Outside songwriters are esteemed in pop and country but less so in hip-hop; outside producers are celebrated in hip-hop but less so in house and techno, where the producer
is
the artist. As the process of music-making has grown more electronic, and therefore more mysterious, the human voice has become more central to ideas of musical authenticity. (Or, rather, the semi-human voice—singers in just about every genre have learned to love Auto-Tune.) Usually, we can treat the person or the group on the album cover as the album’s author, but not always. In the old days, record companies sometimes packaged albums with little or no input from the artists themselves, and K-pop fans still argue over how much creative control their favorite idols really have. Britney Spears is an extreme case: her last three albums were released while she was subject to a legal conservatorship; she later said, of some of the music, “I wasn’t into it.”
Part of the reason for the A.I. backlash is that people worry that this complicated system of attribution will be overwhelmed by a tide of interchangeable, computer-generated songs that weren’t really made by or for anybody. I think that’s unlikely. Most A.I. music tends to be disdained by listeners as inauthentic slop—sometimes because it lacks quality, and more often because it lacks context. On its own, A.I. music is bootleg music—not “bootleg” like an unauthorized live album but “bootleg” like a knockoff pair of sneakers, widely and cheaply available. It hasn’t been claimed by an artist people love or authenticated by a brand that people care about, and so it’s not the real thing. As the Muzak corporation discovered, decades ago, people don’t like to think of themselves as consumers of undifferentiated slop. They want “real” music for the same reason they want “real” Nikes: because they want to feel connected to a tradition, a narrative, a perception of quality, a person.
Sometimes, of course, a bootleg can become authentic. This past summer, when the Knicks won the N.B.A. Finals, a flood of bootleg Knicks T-shirts engulfed the city; years from now, collectors might distinguish a genuine 2026 bootleg (purchased, perhaps, on Seventh Avenue, on the night of the championship) from a worthless knockoff of a knockoff. The designer Dapper Dan, who helped invent hip-hop fashion, was originally known for his high-fashion knockoffs, but consumers came to view him as a brand unto himself. Anyone who hopes to use A.I. technology in a singular and memorable way faces a similar question: How do you make valuable slop?
One answer is: you don’t. Righteous refusal has often been a compelling musical strategy, and sometimes an effective political strategy, too. In the nineteen-forties, the American Federation of Musicians fought for higher royalty rates by going on strike, forbidding its members from making new commercial recordings for more than two years. Today’s pop musicians don’t have that kind of union power, but the A.F.M. is currently suing two of the big labels, Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group, over their deals with A.I. companies. In the meantime, we may see more acts pledging, Queen-like, that their albums contain no A.I., although this disclaimer might be hard to define. Few people seemed to mind when Charli XCX and her producers talked about having used an A.I.-enabled plug-in to stitch together sampled sounds in a recent song. (Especially with instruments, it can be hard to draw a line between A.I.-enhanced and A.I.-generated.) Queen eventually changed its policy on synthesizers—the group’s eighth album, “The Game,” from 1980, began with the eerie, spiralling sound of an Oberheim OB-X. Most listeners have no idea how their favorite songs were made, but, if A.I.-powered musical tools continue to proliferate, eschewing A.I. might soon be less like eschewing synthesizers and more like eschewing electronics altogether: possible, but only for musicians who really want to make a point.
At the other extreme, audiences may learn to love A.I.-generated songs. Pat McAfee, a top sports commentator, recently released a country album, and one of his collaborators, a bona-fide country singer-songwriter named ERNEST, said that the process began with McAfee “chanting” original lyrics into Suno. The album is awful, but pop history is full of examples of memorable music arising from unpromising circumstances; perhaps a celebrity with a more distinctive lyrical sensibility, or a better ability to identify an exceptionally catchy Suno melody, will use these same tools to build a pop career. In music, as elsewhere, curatorial skill may grow more valuable, along with the ability to write a creative A.I. prompt. (If this sounds to you like a musical dystopia, then you can imagine how Sousa would have felt if he’d learned that d.j.s would eventually conquer the world.) Yet outmoded musical expectations have a way of sticking around: listeners still love the sense that their favorite performers are working hard for them. And so anyone who manages to reliably generate popular A.I. songs will be incentivized to act like a musician—to go out and put on some kind of performance, giving audiences a live version of music that was canned to begin with.
That, more or less, was the fate of Fenix Flexin this summer; after about fifteen minutes on the microphone in New Jersey, he headed to Queens for his second club gig of the night. He has been mercilessly roasted online, but the months of non-stop discourse have given “Rubberz” a kind of historical authenticity. The song is now indelibly tied to this summer, a time of excitement and anxiety over A.I.; it is also indelibly tied to the artist behind it, even if he didn’t actually sing it. But, despite its seeming ubiquity, “Rubberz” has been only a modest hit. It peaked at No. 58 on the
Billboard
Hot 100, and remains notably less popular on YouTube and Spotify than the hip-hop hits Fenix Flexin used to be known for. The anti-A.I. movement seems driven by a worry that people will be fooled by slop, but the listening public tends to have strong and rather unpredictable tastes, and also an insatiable hunger for personal connection. It has grown dramatically easier to make a song in the century since Sousa sounded the alarm about proliferating music technology. But it hasn’t grown any easier to make a song that sticks. ♦

epub_30.title: Matisse’s Ugliest Painting
epub_30.text:
Matisse’s Ugliest Painting
The Art World
Matisse’s Ugliest Painting
More than a century after its incendiary début, “Woman with a Hat” remains wonderfully resistant to the dictates of beauty and taste.
By Zachary Fine
August 31, 2026
Matisse’s “Femme au Chapeau” (1905), or “Woman with a Hat,” is a strong contender for my least favorite masterpiece of the twentieth century. When it was first exhibited, in Paris, waves of journalists ridiculed it, viewers laughed and jeered, and at least one person tried to scratch it with their nails. More than enough time has passed to wise up to its charms, but I still can’t reconcile myself to the shock of its ugliness. The painting looks like a box of melted saltwater taffy that’s been churned together and encouraged to express itself as a chic fungus. Leo Stein, the brother of Gertrude, called it “the nastiest smear of paint I had ever seen.” That might sound like an insult, but it’s not. After negotiating with Matisse, the Steins bought the painting at full price.
“Matisse’s Femme au Chapeau: A Modern Scandal,” at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, looks at how a single work sparked a mini-revolution in art. The exhibition’s main room partially re-creates the infamous Gallery VII at the 1905 Salon d’Automne, in the Grand Palais, where Fauvism—the gallery was described as the “
cage aux fauves
,” or “cage of wild beasts”—first congealed into a movement. The room included fifty-five pieces by ten artists, all in their twenties or thirties, most of whom had traded the delicate particles of Impressionist brushwork for meaty strokes of absurd color that corresponded not to reality but to the painter’s own soul. (Or so they implied.)
The entire gallery was a scandal, but the cause célèbre was “Femme au Chapeau”: technically a portrait of Matisse’s wife, Amélie, at age thirty-three. Other Fauves deployed bright, acid colors and sharp contrasts, but their work was either too cozy with Post-Impressionism, as in the wriggling outlines of Maurice de Vlaminck, or too subdued in subject matter, like André Derain’s landscapes, to provoke as much attention. A portrait typically ennobles a sitter—certifying a social rank or commemorating a fondness. When Derain painted Matisse during their fateful sojourn in Collioure, a small coastal village where, in the summer of 1905, they cracked open their palettes and set Fauvism in motion, he gave him warm, peachy skin and a dignified pipe. Not so with Matisse’s portrait of Amélie, whose face is mostly a seasick green. Her spade-shaped jaw and cartoonish eyes barely amount to a likeness. In one sense, “Femme au Chapeau” is a painting
about
painting: a portrait of someone being devoured by paint, not represented by it. But it’s also a portrait of a hat.
Matisse was no stranger to hats. His grandmothers were hatmakers, his aunts were hatmakers, his mother was a hatmaker, and so, too, was Amélie. She opened her own shop in Paris, on Rue de Châteaudun, the year after she and Matisse married, and they lived in the attic above it. One can imagine the kitchen table littered with bobbins, pins, and feathers, as the paraphernalia of the milliner’s life floated up into their private quarters. These were hard years for Matisse: years of professional failure and doubt, when his father shamed him for being an artist and cut off support; years of bronchitis and insomnia, when Amélie would stay up until dawn and read to him; and years of financial strain, when her trade effectively subsidized his. The hat business sustained Matisse and their three children, at least until 1903, when Amélie, in poor health, was forced to close the shop.
Matisse couldn’t have felt neutrally about Amélie making crowns for the same class of wealthy patrons who refused to support him. In the portrait, there’s more than a touch of resentment in the object on her head (
Enough with the hats, Amélie!
)—it’s ridiculous even by late-Belle Époque fashion standards—and there’s some lingering ressentiment, too. As a law student in the eighteen-eighties, Matisse lived on the sixth floor of a cheap hotel in Paris and would use a glass peashooter to fire little balls of putty at the hats of people on the street below. Even before he was “bitten by the demon of painting,” he chafed at the constraints of bourgeois respectability while feeling compelled to uphold them. Hats were a convenient target.
In “Femme au Chapeau,” at least a third of the composition is
chapeau
—and this particular hat is more of a mangled fruit basket, in which nothing is decipherable. The purple tongue sticking out of the top might belong to an iris, and the lobes of reddish orange could be an apple, but they likely aren’t. We’re looking through the eyes of someone who doesn’t want to actually
see
the hat. Matisse’s project was to wrench the appearance of things, particularly their colors, away from reality, and to let them entertain a new internal correspondence guided by his expressive whims. It’s a childish way to thank the world for its visual bounty, but he knew that. Reminiscing about his summer with Derain, Matisse said, “We were at that point like children before nature, and we let our temperaments speak. . . . I spoiled everything on principle, and worked as I felt, only by color.” The desire to spoil, to transgress on principle, to
épater le bourgeois
—those are the words of the avant-garde artist.
There’s a well-manicured story about Matisse becoming a modern painter—the drift from conservative academies and salons toward eccentric splinter groups; the pixelated brushwork transmitted through Paul Signac; the seductiveness of Cézanne; the plunges into southern light in Corsica, Saint-Tropez, and Collioure—but I worry that this sketch has numbed us to the specific case of “Femme au Chapeau,” which is much more temperamental and, well,
freakish
than what the artist made before and after. Matisse spent months working on a different painting for the 1905 Salon d’Automne: a landscape, filled with formulaic dashes and carefully modulated color contrasts, called “The Port of Abail.” He tossed it aside and in a matter of weeks whipped up “Femme au Chapeau” as a substitute—the brilliance of one painting released by the frustration of another. In the years on either side of “Femme au Chapeau,” Matisse painted two Arcadian fantasies, “Luxe, Calme et Volupté” (1904) and “Le Bonheur de Vivre” (1906), that show his style trending toward flat, simplified forms and liquid arabesques. Those paintings affirm Matisse’s reputation as modern art’s ultimate pleasure-seeker—the man who famously said that art should be like a “good armchair,” and whose studios had a tendency to evaporate the clothes of women.
The portrait of Madame Matisse, by contrast, is an anxious smear job. Generally, a painting’s Fauvist credentials rely on at least three factors: the use of nonmimetic color (e.g., no worldly skin tones or blue water); the contrast of complementary colors to balance the picture (red and green, orange and blue, etc.); and the flat application of “pure” color, as opposed to subtle shades, with each patch marking a Cézanne-like shift in plane (i.e., hue, more than line, structuring the space). What’s odd is that Matisse’s painting doesn’t abide by any of these rules, at least not entirely. Unlike his other high-Fauve entry in the 1905 salon, “Open Window, Collioure,” which uses a palette of pinks and mint greens to establish clean contrasts, “Femme au Chapeau” permits no easy pleasures. The painting is filled with inconsistencies and bizarre compensatory moves. Its attitude can be summarized by a single square inch at the base of Amélie’s neck, where one finds eight colors in competition: orange, yellow, blue, white, teal, apricot, pale brown, and some black, as underdrawing.
Matisse takes every opportunity to disturb passages of chromatic balance. The red hair that connects with the green of Amélie’s temple? It’s interrupted by a few strokes of magenta, to increase the tension. The blue of the hat’s brim? A splash of teal agitates its roundness. While some of the color contrasts do articulate planar shifts, such as the candy-stripe lips (red for upper, pink for lower), many of the touches are arbitrary splotches that neither bolster a shape nor set another off. I have to imagine that Matisse was tickled by his decision to put a large tract of green in front of Madame’s face and, instead of extending it all the way to her throat, suddenly introduce a purple goatee.
The aspect of the painting that troubles me most, though, is the sleeve of Amélie’s dress. Fauvism was supposedly characterized by the phasing out of the Neo-Impressionist
tache
, or uniformly pointillist stroke—abundant in “Luxe, Calme et Volupté” and “The Port of Abail”—in favor of broader patches of color, but the green sleeve, with its cobra-headed cuff, is a creepy disturbance to the brushwork elsewhere. Compared with the thick smudges of white on the fan that Amélie is holding, or the broad, lush strokes of the background, the sleeve is fidgety. None of its marks seem to maintain their integrity for more than an inch or two without being fretted or spoiled. There’s a slight air of death around it, as if the arm is deteriorating in front of us.
Part of the greatness of “Femme au Chapeau” is the endurance of its ugliness. Most ugly things are easy to assimilate or neutralize in time. But Matisse made sure to create enough visual friction to prevent that from happening. The composure of Amélie, and the decidedly wild and clownish manner in which she’s painted, can’t be tamed into order, elegance, or beauty. There’s also no golden picture frame or change in fashion that will make the painting’s bourgeois genre (portraiture) comport with its over-the-top accessory (the hat). The hat is destined to be hideous and interesting, and the painting is determined to be
too much
—too colorful, too self-conscious of its own materials, “excessively modern,” as one person put it. That was in 1905. Lucky for us, the painting still is. ♦

In “Adults,” Gen Z Gets the Hangout Sitcom It Deserves
On Television
In “Adults,” Gen Z Gets the Hangout Sitcom It Deserves
The FX series, which is returning for a second season, won’t restore the genre to its normcore roots—but, happily, it has no interest in doing so.
By Inkoo Kang
August 27, 2026
The twentysomething protagonists of the Gen Z hangout comedy “Adults” understand that growing up sometimes requires an intervention. In the first episode of the new season, which premières this week, five housemates gather in their living room to conduct what they’ve dubbed the Scrub: the act of identifying and erasing their most employment-endangering social-media posts, under the credo that you must “bury your past before it buries you.” A clip of Samir (Malik Elassal) as a teen-ager, comforting a female celebrity through the power of dance after Trump’s first election? Delete. A YouTube video of Issa (Amita Rao) counting down the “top ten worst accents”?
Definite
delete. “It’s not our fault we got the internet when we were our most horny and stupid,” Samir protests. Yes, it’s an exercise in humiliation—but it’s the kind of lesson you’d rather get from your nearest and dearest than from an H.R. department. And it fits right into the time-honored sitcom tradition of needing a little help from your friends.
Television’s great crowd-pleasers used to hinge on such chemistry and warmth. In the early nineties, the writers David Crane and Marta Kauffman pitched NBC on the then relatively novel insight that “when you’re single and in the city, your friends are your family.” The result of this epiphany was “Friends,” a ratings juggernaut that remains improbably popular three decades later. The formula that show cemented—of idealistic urbanites, often with more education than experience, getting mired in low-stakes high jinks—led to such notable successors as “How I Met Your Mother,” which débuted in 2005, and “New Girl,” in 2011. Eventually, the young-people-doing-nothing format got the prestige treatment, with 2012’s “Girls” (which admittedly owes as much to “Sex and the City”) and 2014’s “Broad City.” These edgier entries reflected the dominant cultural forces of their era: cringe comedy and exuberant feminism, respectively.
Since then, the hangout sitcom has suffered a precipitous decline. Its native structure, the twenty-two-episode season, has become a rarity in the industry, as has its default lightness. But the genre is mounting a comeback. “Adults” is part of this Zoomer revamp, along with Rachel Sennott’s pricklier “I Love LA”—the “Seinfeld” to “Adults” ’s “Friends”—and Mindy Kaling’s creakier “Not Suitable for Work.” Whereas Rachel and Monica’s misadventures in “Friends” ultimately spanned a decade or so in the city, “Adults” seems hyper-focussed on that fabled sliver of one’s twenties before ambition or even romance sets in—when life is composed almost entirely of side quests, and deciding on a main quest is still a few years away. The show’s central quintet reside in the childhood home of Samir, whose semi-retired parents are on an apparently indefinite tour of the national parks. Samir allows his friends to live with him for free while he works as a food-delivery driver—a gig that he’s happy to put on pause when the opportunity arises to play video games with some teen-age boys who’ve used the app to order beer. Guests—defined loosely as anyone from a random hookup to Julia Fox to a surprisingly chill raccoon—drop by the house with regularity, creating a zippy blend of the mundane and the serendipitous.
The married creators of “Adults,” Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw, seem well aware of the lineage of their series. (At one point, a character played by the “Girls” star Zosia Mamet asks one of the protagonists, “You think you’re the first people to be young and adorable in New York?”) Perhaps that’s why the pair has striven to create fresh archetypes. The most fully realized personalities are Anton (Owen Thiele), a compulsive charmer who needs to make every passing acquaintance feel as though they’ve forged a lasting connection, and Billie (Lucy Freyer), a former overachiever who’s lost without the structure of school. (Offscreen, Billie may be singlehandedly keeping the gifted-child-meme industry alive by liking every post about smart kids who never live up to their potential.) But other characters verge on parody. Issa, an overconfident blusterer whom Samir and Anton met in college, seems to be stuck doing a one-note Ilana Glazer impression; her boyfriend, Paul Baker (Jack Innanen), who’s always referred to by his full name, is distinguished only by being Canadian, sexually fluid, and nice.
“Adults” won’t be the hangout show that restores the genre to its normcore, network-friendly roots—if such a return is even viable in the current comedy landscape. Happily, it’s not trying to be. Its politics lean unapologetically left; like “Girls” and “Broad City” before it, “Adults” features an irreverent abortion subplot. It also eschews the heteronormativity of its predecessors: Anton is gay, Billie sleeps with both men and women, and the show’s primary will-they-won’t-they couple is queer. One half of that would-be pairing is Paul Baker, whose softboi credentials come into question when it emerges that he has a second, markedly straighter friend group—a pack of testicle-slapping bros promptly labelled the Shame Friends.
The divide sets up the kind of ethnography at which “Adults” excels. In the Season 2 première, a riotous piece of generational social taxonomy, this other crew tries haplessly to cater to the tastes and mores of the main group, with one dude donning a “directed by Greta Gerwig” T-shirt and later declaring, “I have mental health!” But there’s also a subtle rejection of the earnest wokeness of years past. The diversity of the core ensemble—a far cry from Hannah Horvath’s all-white friend group—is rarely remarked upon by the characters, except as part of a bit. The show itself acknowledges their identities only obliquely, as in an episode where an exhausted Anton forgets to code switch at his corporate job and praises a colleague’s presentation by chirping, “Cunt alert!” Naturally, the rest of the plot focusses on his elaborate scheme to get out of hot water by normalizing the word in his office.
Each successive generation since “Friends” has seen its sitcom youths diminished in their circumstances. Rachel and Monica’s West Village sublet gave way to Hannah and Marnie’s Greenpoint apartment—an address that might be considered laughably unattainable by the broke twentysomethings of today. The most original element of “Adults” is its setting: a cozy single-family house in outer Queens, filled with the décor choices of a middle-aged mom, all floral patterns and ornately carved furniture. Though the home is a haven for Samir and his friends, it is pointedly not theirs. “Adults” doesn’t dwell on the contingency of the characters’ housing situation, but economic struggle is the show’s unmistakable backdrop. It’s evident in the sheer number of scenes that take place in the living room or the kitchen. While earlier sitcom crews met up at a coffee shop or a bar, young people like Billie—who spends her days submitting dozens of job applications without a single reply—are scarcely in a position to treat the city as their playground.
Such worries are more prominent in the superior second season, which finds some of the friends engaging in that perpetual hobbyhorse of the young: fretting about no longer being as young as they used to be. Billie’s anxieties about her lack of accomplishments at twenty-five are exacerbated by meeting the infinitely cooler girl who now uses her old fake I.D., and the typically even-keeled Anton can’t help regressing into a shrieking brat in the presence of his older sister (Raven-Symoné). These story lines add a sense of urgency and progress to a series that was a little too comfortable being amiably aimless. The shift feels like the show finding its footing in a more traditional sitcom register.
Kronengold and Shaw rarely falter in coming up with unique plotlines and sharply observed jokes. But, compared with its forebears, which gradually accrued emotional power as their characters matured together, “Adults” seems strangely reluctant to delve into the inner lives of young people whose hearts may never again be so open or vulnerable. In the first season, for instance, Billie’s fear that she peaked in high school leads to an ill-advised fling with her middle-aged journalism teacher. The relationship ends in calamity, of course, but the series spends little time wondering what she gleaned from the experience. When the friends do divulge deeper secrets to one another, they often instruct the hearer to “mind wipe”: to listen to the revelation, then pretend as if they never did. Like the Scrub, it’s a self-protective gesture, designed to mitigate risk. But we can get to know the characters only so well when they’re doing their best not to know themselves. ♦

Just Kidding
Poems
Just Kidding
By Rita Dove
August 30, 2026
A priest, a rabbi, and a poet walk into a bar
and we’re laughing already, calculating their clashing philosophies—
New Testament, the Torah, W. B. Yeats—all
the earnest sacraments undertaken in the name of world harmony:
loaves & fishes, bitter herbs, the spread offered at the free buffet.
We’ve even uploaded their wardrobes
(dog collar, skullcap, jeans & elbow-patched tweed)
as we wait for the next line’s classic setup for ridicule,
because we know the poet’s gonna be the one to rip
this sucker apart; it’s always the last one through the door
who gets the biggest laugh.
But we’ve forgotten the bar! There it stands,
waiting to be leaned on, a gleaming walnut shoulder
anointed with Scotch and spittle. Poor bar!
Elbowed, drooled over, kicked and beslobbered,
its whisky-ring tattoos a parade of evenings
lost to sorrow, to rage, the occasional pickup—
Are you uncomfortable yet? Itching in your seat,
muttering,
Where’s the fun in this? It’s the poet’s doing
—
they can turn bread into zwieback, wine into vinegar
,
claim edification in the name of one lousy epiphany.
When’s it coming, the goddam punch line?
Oooof! There goes one to the gut.
A priest, a rabbi, and a poet at the bar. What’ll it be?
Old-Fashioned, Negroni, Moscow Mule—you decide.
They don’t speak. They aren’t acquainted. They just
happen to need something stronger than what’s out there
and enter the same establishment at the same time—10
p.m.
—
where the bartender, wiping away some previous patron’s ablutions,
asks: “What’s your poison?”—to which
the priest thinks:
Angel’s Envy
,
the rabbi murmurs:
Killer Whale
,
the poet sighs:
I’ve drawn a blank
,
just fill me up
—
and the bartender sets down their drinks with a half-mast salute
to these disparate, desperate creatures
who already know they’re the butt of the joke
and gamely take the hit.

Poems
Horse Song of a Nightmare
By Joy Harjo
August 30, 2026
It is raining, raining, raining.
The sky is falling, falling, falling.
I never, never, never.
Saw this would happen, happen, happen.
As in any flooding, flooding, flooding.
The earth is breaking, breaking, breaking.
All the sorrow, sorrow, sorrow, kneeling.
Inside the loss and anger kindling.
Set forth the burning, burning, burning.
On this earthly star shining, shining, shining.
Then we lost our footing, footing, footing.
Again the falling, falling, falling.
Into a nightmare running, running, running.
On black horses riding, riding, riding.
Through darkness in the raining, raining, raining.
Then there we were standing, standing, standing.
On the grassy hump of dawning, dawning, dawning.
Over the mountains rainy, rainy, rainy.
The clouds leaned down to sing.
This is drawn from “
Cloud Runner
.”
